This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action amends geographic coordinates for boundary points listed in the airspace descriptions for restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C to correct minor discrepancies that resulted in gaps and overlaps between the areas. This action does not expand any external boundaries or change any altitudes, times of designation, or activities conducted within the restricted areas.
DATES:
Effective date 0901 UTC, December 24, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of this final rule and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document
( printed page 65108)
may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ashley Toth, Airspace Regulation Group, Operational Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for this Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it amends the coordinates for restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C in North Carolina to close small gaps and eliminate overlaps between the restricted areas.
Background
The FAA recently conducted a review of restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C, revealing minor discrepancies in the points defining the areas. The FAA identified small gaps and overlap points based on the coordinates used in the boundary descriptions, which necessitates this amendment to accurately align the restricted areas. Moreover, the U.S. Marine Corps, the using agency, requested that the FAA amend the coordinates to eliminate these gaps and overlaps.
Good Cause for Bypassing Notice and Comment
Under 5 U.S.C. 553, federal agencies engaged in informal rulemaking must provide the public with a notice of proposed rulemaking and an opportunity for public participation. However, 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) exempts a rule from these requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Courts have construed these exceptions narrowly, but have nonetheless accepted determinations of good cause that notice and comment is unnecessary in “those situations in which the administrative rule is a routine determination, insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry and to the public.”
See Mack Trucks, Inc.
v.
EPA,
682 F.3d 87, 94 (D.C. Cir. 2012). This action consists of minor technical amendments only. It does not affect the external boundaries or change the altitudes, time of designation, operating requirements, or activities conducted in the restricted areas. Therefore, the FAA finds good cause that notice and public procedure under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) are unnecessary.
The Rule
This action amends 14 CFR part 73 by updating the coordinates used in the boundary descriptions to accurately align restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C, eliminating gaps and overlaps. The first coordinate listed in R-5301 is changed from “lat. 36°04′56″ N, long. 76°16′47″ W” to “lat. 36°04′56″ N, long. 76°16′48″ W”. Two tie-in coordinates are added to R-5302B, “lat. 36°04′23″ N, long. 076°20′59″ W” to “lat. 36°04′56″ N, long. 076°16′48″ W”, to eliminate overlap and provide coincidence with R-5301. Finally, an additional tie-in coordinate is added to R-5302B and R-5302C, “lat. 36°00′01″ N, long. 76°14′29″ W”, to eliminate overlap and provide coincidence with R-5302A.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedures” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is anticipated to have a minimal economic impact, as it only affects air traffic procedures and air navigation, resulting in at most de minimis costs from minor rerouting of flights. Since this is a routine matter that only affects air traffic procedures with de minimis impact on operators, it is certified that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action of making an administrative change of updating the coordinates used in the boundary descriptions to accurately align restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C, NC, eliminating gaps and overlaps, qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. 4321et seq.) and in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G,
FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,
paragraph B-2.5 (d) Modification of the technical description of special use airspace (SUA) that does not alter the dimensions, altitudes, or times of designation of the airspace (such as changes in designation of the controlling or using agency, or correction of typographical errors). As such, this action is not expected to result in any potentially significant environmental impacts. AGENCY:
Federal Maritime Commission.
ACTION:
Sixty-day notice; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, and as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the Federal Maritime Commission (Commission) invites comments on the continuing information collections related to Carrier Automated Tariffs and related form, FMC-1. This notice announces a renewal of an existing collection and includes updates to the collection based on the increase in the number of response and burden hours for respondents; and a new electronic platform to submit the Form FMC-1.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The Commission is accepting comments using the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov.
The docket for this notice, which includes copies of applicable forms and submitted comments, can be found at
www.regulations.gov
under the FMC-2026-0431. Follow the instructions provided for submitting comments.
The Commission invites the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on any aspect of the continuing information collection listed in this notice, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.). We are particularly interested in receiving comments on: (1) the necessity and utility of the proposed information collection for the proper performance of the agency's functions; (2) the accuracy of the estimated burden; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology to minimize the information collection burden.
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be included or summarized in our request for Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval of the relevant information collection. All comments are part of the public record and subject to disclosure. Please do not include any confidential or inappropriate material in your comments.
Information Collections Open for Comment
Title:46 CFR part 520—Carrier Automated Tariffs and Related Form FMC-1.
OMB Control Number:
3072-0064 (Expires January 31, 2027).
Form Numbers:
FMC-1.
Abstract:
Except with respect to certain specified commodities, section 8(a) of the Shipping Act of 1984, 46 U.S.C. 40501(a)-(c), requires that each common carrier and conference shall keep open to public inspection, in an automated tariff system, tariffs showing its rates, charges, classifications, rules, and practices between all ports and points on its own route and on any through transportation route that has been established. In addition, individual carriers or agreements among carriers are required to make available in tariff format certain enumerated essential terms of their service contracts. 46 U.S.C. 40502. The Commission is responsible for reviewing the accessibility and accuracy of automated tariff systems, in accordance with its regulations set forth at 46 CFR part 520.
Type of Review:
Extension with change.
Current Actions:
The estimated number of responses and the burden hours for the collection have increased due to an increase in the number of respondents. Form FMC-1 continues to be submitted electronically but has been included with the agency's modernization initiative and will be included within the ServiceNow platform.
Needs and Uses:
The Commission uses information obtained from Form FMC-1 to ascertain the location of common carrier and conference tariff publications and to access their provisions regarding rules, rates, charges and practices.
Frequency:
This information is collected when common carriers or conferences publish tariffs.
Type of Respondents:
Persons desiring to operate as common carriers or conferences.
Number of Annual Respondents:
The Commission estimates there are 9,324 Carrier Automated Tariffs. It is estimated that the number of annual responses will be 189,134.
Estimated Time per Response:
The time per response ranges from 0.017 to 2 person-hours for reporting and recordkeeping requirements contained in the rules, and is estimated at 0.25
( printed page 65554)
person-hours for completing Form FMC-1.
Total Annual Burden:
The Commission estimates the total person-hour burden at 4,740.03 hours.

articles.title: Why Asian FDI is flowing into northern Vietnam’s industrial parks - Vietnam Investment Review - VIR
articles.summary: Why Asian FDI is flowing into northern Vietnam’s industrial parks  Vietnam Investment Review - VIR
articles.full_text:
In northern Vietnam, alongside major industrial hubs such as Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Park (VSIP), DEEP C, and Trang Due, new projects such as An Phat 5 Industrial Park are helping strengthen Haiphong city’s position as a destination for foreign investment.
Global supply chain diversification has prompted Asian businesses to relocate manufacturing facilities to Vietnam in recent years, particularly in supporting industries, electronic components and AI-related manufacturing.
This trend is not only generating additional demand for industrial land but also raising expectations for infrastructure quality and logistics connectivity at industrial parks (IPs). As global supply chains are restructured, northern Vietnam is stepping up investment in transport infrastructure.
| Artist’s impression of the mega-project Gia Binh International Airport, with initial facilities scheduled for completion in time for APEC 2027. Photo: An Phat Holdings | 
According to Cushman & Wakefield’s Northern Key Economic Zone Industrial Markets Q2/2026 report, northern Vietnam’s cumulative industrial land supply exceeded 25,200 hectares at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up 15.7 per cent on-year.
Haiphong accounted for the largest share, at 26 per cent of total supply, followed by Bac Ninh with 21 per cent. In the ready-built factory segment, the occupancy rate remained at 86 per cent, indicating sustained demand for manufacturing facilities that can be brought into operation quickly.
Against this backdrop, northern Vietnam is accelerating investment in strategic transport infrastructure. A notable project is Gia Binh International Airport, which is planned to meet ICAO Code 4F standards, with an expected annual capacity of 30 million passengers and 1.6 million tonnes of cargo by 2030.
At the same time, the road linking Gia Binh Airport with Hanoi and the Ring Road 4 project in the Capital Region are being fast-tracked. These projects are expected to strengthen connectivity among key industrial centres, including Hanoi, Bac Ninh and Haiphong, while improving access to international markets.
Notably, several infrastructure components are being expedited with a view to bringing them into operation in phases in 2027.
Over the longer term, shorter travel times between manufacturing centres, seaports and aviation gateways will improve transport efficiency and create a competitive advantage for new IP projects in northern Vietnam, including An Phat 5 Industrial Park (Luong Dien–Ngoc Lien) in Haiphong city, developed within the An Phat Holdings’ ecosystem.
| Land at An Phat 5 Industrial Park is ready for handover to investors. Photo: An Phat Holdings | 
According to a representative of An Phat Complex, essential infrastructure at An Phat 5 IP which covers 150 ha in Cam Giang commune (Haiphong city) is largely complete, and cleared plots can be handed over to investors in phases.
The entire infrastructure system is expected to be completed in 2026, with the project being developed as a model IP in compliance with environmental, social and governance standards and targeting integrated operations from Q1 of 2027.
As Vietnam gradually transforms into a global manufacturing hub, An Phat 5 IP is actively broadening its reach to Asian investors seeking to expand production capacity.
The project is positioned as a high-tech, innovation-driven IP targeting businesses in electrical and electronic equipment, IT, mechanical engineering and machinery manufacturing, automation, supporting industries, construction materials and other suitable industrial manufacturing sectors.
| An Phat Complex was introduced at Vietnam-China Trade, Investment and Technology Cooperation Forum in Nanning, China, on September 17. Photo: An Phat Holdings | 
From an investor’s perspective, strategic location and logistics connectivity are key considerations when selecting a site for a manufacturing facility.
A Chinese investor said, “We chose An Phat 5 because of its convenient connectivity between Haiphong and China via road, sea and rail networks, which helps optimise the import of raw materials and export of finished products. In particular, infrastructure development at the project is progressing on schedule, enabling businesses to plan their production activities.”
The implementation capabilities and infrastructure development experience of An Phat Complex have been demonstrated through projects such as An Phat Complex and An Phat 1 IP, as well as its cooperation with international companies including Biel Crystal, Ce-Link and Sumida.
An Phat 5 IP is well positioned to translate its infrastructure advantages and strategic location into tangible investment appeal, helping reinforce Haiphong city’s standing amid the global shift in manufacturing.
| An Phat 5 Industrial Park (Luong Dien–Ngoc Lien) The project is developed by An Phat High-Tech Industrial Park JSC (An Phat Complex), a member of An Phat Holdings. It was approved for investment in the construction and operation of An Phat 5 Industrial Park’s infrastructure in Haiphong city under Decision No. 1008/QD-TTg dated August 31, 2023. Address: Km 28+125, National Highway No.38, Cam Giang commune, Haiphong city. Total area: 150 hectares. Operating term: 50 years, until 2073. Regional connectivity: 40km (40 minutes) from Hanoi; 55km (60 minutes) from Noi Bai International Airport; 12km (20 minutes) from Gia Binh International Airport; and 65km (90 minutes) from Haiphong International Port. Bac Ninh, Hung Yen and Haiphong’s centre are all accessible within approximately 60 minutes. Contact the developer: Hotline: (+84) 902 046 969 \| (+84) 906 077 57 Email: info@anphatcomplex.com |

articles.summary: "At This Rate, South Korea Could Be Left with Nowhere to Stand"... Chinese Cars Break Through Tariff Barriers and Spread Worldwide [China Shock, K Industry on the Brink | Automobiles] (3)  아시아경제
articles.full_text:
[China Shock, Korean Industry on the Brink | Automobiles] ③ China Expands Production Bases from Emerging Markets to Europe, with Parts Makers Joining the "Human-Wave" Push
BYD Expands Beyond India and Thailand to Hungary and North America
Chery Begins Local Production in Spain
Weak Domestic Demand Drives Expansion of Overseas Production
Cutting Tariffs and Logistics Costs Nearly Halves Prices
Battery and Par
China, once known as the "factory of the world," is now penetrating auto markets around the globe by building factories in numerous countries. The country is expanding production bases beyond Southeast Asia to Brazil and Europe, moving beyond mass production at home and low-priced exports. Its strategy is to overcome tariff barriers by building local factories and acquiring existing production facilities, while establishing overseas supply chains through the expansion of battery and auto parts companies alongside automakers.
The expansion of China's auto industry overseas poses a threat to the positions of both South Korean automakers and auto parts makers. If Chinese companies lower prices through local production, South Korean automakers will face greater price competition in key export markets. As Chinese parts makers that expand overseas alongside automakers broaden their supply relationships with global automakers, competition among South Korean parts makers to secure orders is also expected to intensify.
According to the Korea Automobile Research Institute on October 15, at least 15 Chinese auto and parts manufacturers announced overseas projects from October 2025 through early 2026. As of February this year, planned investments totaled around 70 billion yuan.
Production bases expand around the world, from emerging markets to Europe
Chinese companies are expanding their production bases from emerging markets such as Thailand, Brazil and Indonesia to Europe. BYD is increasing local production in Thailand and Brazil, among other countries, and has also been pursuing construction of a factory in Hungary. Chery Automobile has begun production in Spain, while Geely and Xpeng are also seeking to secure production facilities in Europe.
Tighter trade regulations are driving the expansion of overseas production. In 2024, the European Union (EU) imposed additional countervailing duties on electric vehicles made in China. Thailand is strengthening local production requirements relative to imported vehicles in connection with its electric vehicle subsidy program, while Brazil is also gradually raising tariffs on electric vehicle imports, with rates set to reach 35% in 2026. Maintaining price competitiveness solely by exporting vehicles made in China has become more difficult.
Local production helps reduce tariff burdens and logistics costs, and makes it easier to meet local sourcing requirements. According to data from the Korea Automobile Research Institute, the price of the standard BYD Atto 3 sold in Thailand fell from 1.1 million baht in 2022 to around 630,000 baht after local production began. In Indonesia, the price of the MG4 electric vehicle, previously imported as a fully assembled vehicle, dropped from 690 million rupiah to 430 million rupiah after production shifted locally. If Chinese companies also lower production costs overseas, South Korean automakers selling vehicles in the same markets could face greater pressure to compete on price.
Weak domestic demand is also driving efforts to target overseas markets. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), domestic auto sales in China totaled 13.162 million units from January through August this year, down 21.8% from the same period a year earlier.
Exports, by contrast, have emerged as a growth driver. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), China's auto exports totaled 7.45 million units over the same period, up 51% year over year. Exports of new energy vehicles reached 3.46 million units, an increase of 70%. Total exports in August were 1.05 million units, 37% higher than in the same month last year. The CPCA forecasts that overseas sales by China's auto industry will exceed 12 million units this year, up about 44% from 8.3 million last year.
Batteries and parts makers expand overseas, building supply chains near Europe
Following automakers, battery and auto parts makers, including those specializing in electronic components and chassis, are also securing production facilities near major markets. Morocco, in particular, is emerging as a new base for Chinese parts makers. The country is close to Europe, offers access to free trade agreements (FTAs), and has advantages in land and labor costs as well as taxation.
When automakers' production facilities and parts supply chains move overseas together, Chinese companies can supply parts to vehicles produced locally while also expanding business with global customers. This is likely to intensify competition for orders between South Korean parts makers and Chinese companies seeking to supply global automakers.
Chinese companies have also made notable gains in global auto parts rankings. The 2026 ranking of the world's 100 largest auto parts suppliers, published by U.S. automotive trade publication Automotive News, included 17 Chinese companies, two more than the 15 listed in 2025. China ranked second, behind Japan with 23 companies, and ahead of the United States with 16 and Germany with 15. The ranking was based on original equipment (OE) sales to automakers.
CATL, the world's largest battery maker, ranked third, with 2025 OE sales of $44.058 billion, up about 25% from the previous year. Yanfeng, a Chinese automotive interiors company, ranked 15th. Chinese companies across a range of fields, including interiors and automotive electronics as well as batteries, made the top 100.

articles.title: India-New Zealand FTA Rules of Origin: Tariff Eligibility and Transit Rules - India Briefing
articles.summary: India-New Zealand FTA Rules of Origin: Tariff Eligibility and Transit Rules  India Briefing
articles.full_text:
India has notified the Customs Tariff (Determination of Origin of Goods under the Free Trade Agreement between India and New Zealand) Rules, 2026. The dossier establishes the conditions goods must meet to qualify for preferential customs duty treatment under the India-New Zealand FTA.
Issued through Notification No. 82/2026-Customs (N.T.) on 12 October 2026, the rules come into force on 20 October 2026.
For businesses trading between India and New Zealand, products must satisfy the applicable origin criteria. Also, importers and exporters must follow proper documentation requirements and consignment conditions to qualify for preferential treatment.
Evaluate Trade Benefits
Assess product-level tariff treatment, rules-of-origin requirements, and potential savings under the India-New Zealand FTA.
What are the India-New Zealand FTA Rules of Origin 2026?
The Rules of Origin establish whether goods qualify as originating in India or New Zealand for preferential customs duty treatment under the FTA. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) notified the rules under Section 5(1) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.
The rules cover:
- Origin criteria for wholly obtained and manufactured goods
- Product-specific rules (PSR) based on the HS 2022 classification
- Qualifying value content (QVC) calculations and material valuation
- Bilateral cumulation and allowances for non-originating materials
- Certificates of Origin and origin declarations
- Importer obligations and post-importation refund claims
- Record retention, customs verification, and penalties for non-compliance
CLICK HERE: India-New Zealand FTA: What Business Opportunities Does the Agreement Offer?
What are the product-specific rules of origin under India-New Zealand FTA?
Annexure A specifies the origin requirements for products based on their HS 2022 classification. Depending on the product, these rules may require:
- Wholly obtained (WO): The product must be wholly obtained or produced in India or New Zealand.
- Change in tariff classification (CC, CTH, or CTSH): Non-originating materials must undergo the specified change in HS classification during production.
- Qualifying value content (QVC): The product must meet a minimum value-content threshold.
- Specified process: Commodity must undergo a prescribed manufacturing process.
Some products must meet a combination of these requirements, while others may qualify by meeting one of several alternatives.
How is QVC calculated under the India-New Zealand FTA?
QVC measures the qualifying value attributable to a product under the applicable origin rule. Where a PSR prescribes a QVC threshold, Rule 6 permits two calculation methods.
- Build-down method: The build-down method deducts the value of non-originating materials from the product’s free-on-board (FOB) value.
Formula: QVC = [(FOB value − value of non-originating materials) ÷ FOB value] × 100
- Build-up method: The build-up method calculates the proportion of the FOB value represented by originating materials.
Formula: QVC = (Value of originating materials ÷ FOB value) × 100
Does the India-New Zealand FTA rules of origin allow bilateral cumulation?
Yes. Rule 5 permits bilateral cumulation between India and New Zealand.
Under this provision, a material that qualifies as originating in one Party may be treated as originating in the other when incorporated into a product there, provided the applicable requirements are satisfied.
For example, a New Zealand manufacturer may use a qualifying Indian-originating component in a finished product. The component may count as originating for the relevant assessment under the cumulation rules.
Cumulation does not automatically confer originating status on every imported input. Businesses must establish the material’s origin and retain supporting documentation.
What is the de minimis rule?
Rule 9 provides limited tolerance for certain non-originating materials that prevent a product from meeting a change-in-tariff-classification requirement.
The applicable limits are:
- Goods outside HS Chapters 50-63: Relevant non-originating materials must generally not exceed 10 per cent of the product’s FOB value.
- Goods under HS Chapters 50-63: Relevant non-originating materials must not exceed 10 per cent of the product’s total weight or value.
- Certain wholly obtained goods: A separate 1 per cent tolerance applies in specified cases involving non-originating materials from other HS chapters.
The de minimis rule does not waive other origin requirements.
Which operations do not confer origin?
Rule 8 identifies operations that are insufficient, either individually or in combination, to establish originating status. These include:
- Preserving goods for transport or storage
- Packaging goods or preparing them for transportation or sale
- Simple sorting, screening, cutting, grinding, bending, or similar operations
- Affixing or printing labels, marks, logos, and other distinguishing signs
- Simple dilution, assembly, disassembly, mixing, painting, or polishing
- Certain textile finishing operations
- Slaughtering animals, as specified in the rule
The rules require relevant operations carried out in a Party to be considered together when assessing whether processing is insufficient. Consequently, importing goods and merely packaging, labelling, or performing simple assembly in India or New Zealand does not automatically make them originating goods.
Can goods shipped through a third country retain origin?
Yes. Rule 15 allows originating goods to retain their status when transported through a third country, provided the prescribed conditions are met.
Goods must not undergo further production or other operations outside India and New Zealand, except for permitted activities such as unloading, reloading, storage, repacking, specified relabelling, splitting or consolidating loads, and operations necessary to preserve or transport them. The goods must also remain under customs control in the third country.
Under Rule 15(2) and (3), the importer must be able to demonstrate compliance when requested by the importing country’s customs administration. Evidence may include:
- Customs documents issued by the transit country
- Bills of lading or airway bills
- Multimodal or combined transport documents
- A non-manipulation certificate
- Other relevant supporting documents requested by customs
For example, an Indian-originating product routed through Singapore to New Zealand may retain its originating status if the transit and customs-control conditions are satisfied.
What proof of origin is required under the India-New Zealand FTA?
Rule 16 recognises two forms of proof of origin:
- Certificate of Origin issued by an authorised authority
- Origin declaration completed by an eligible declarant.
A Certificate of Origin must include an authorised signature, an official seal, and the information prescribed in Annexure B. The declaration must include the details specified in Annexure C and a unique identification number.
The documents must also include relevant details such as the exporter, importer, HS code, goods description, shipment, origin criteria, weight, and invoice references.
Can an importer claim a refund after importation?
Yes. Rule 25 permits a post-importation claim where the importer did not claim preferential treatment at importation, but the goods qualified at that time.
The claim must include the required proof of origin, import documentation, and supporting information. The normal deadline is 12 months from importation, subject to any longer period permitted under domestic law.
If an importer discovers that a claim was incorrect, the relevant import documentation must be corrected and additional duties and applicable penalties paid.
How long must origin records be retained?
Rule 23 requires relevant origin records to be retained for at least five years, or longer where domestic law requires.
Exporters, producers, approved exporters, status holders, and issuing authorities must maintain records necessary to demonstrate originating status. Importers must retain records supporting the origin of goods for which preferential treatment was claimed.
Relevant records may include:
- Bills of materials and supplier declarations
- Purchase invoices and import documentation for materials
- Production records and process descriptions
- Material cost breakdowns and QVC calculations
- Freight, insurance, and other valuation documents
- Certificates of Origin or origin declarations
- Bills of landing, airway bills, and other transport documents
Supporting records may be maintained electronically, digitally, or in writing, provided they remain retrievable and comply with applicable domestic law.
What is the customs verification process for origin claims?
Rule 26 permits customs administrations to verify origin claims at importation or after release. The process may involve requests to an issuing authority, exporter, producer, approved exporter, or status holder. Customs may also seek permission to conduct a verification visit.
| Key Customs Verification Timelines under India-New Zealand FTA |  | 
| Verification action | Timeline | 
| Verification of certificate authenticity | Response within 30 days | 
| Inquiry into a suspected inaccurate origin determination | Response within 60 days, extendable by up to 30 days | 
| Direct information request | Response within 60 days, extendable by up to 30 days | 
| Consent for a verification visit | Preferential treatment may be denied if consent is not obtained within 30 days after the authority receives the request | 
| Written determination following a verification visit | Within six months from the date the visit was conducted | 
| Comments following an adverse written determination | Within 30 days of receipt | 
| Final determination after comments | Within 30 days of receiving the comments or additional information |

articles.title: The Canadian economy is facing double pressure from US tariffs and rising energy prices. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Canadian economy is facing double pressure from US tariffs and rising energy prices.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The Canadian economy is under pressure from tariffs and energy prices, forcing the country to accelerate the diversification of export markets, remove domestic trade barriers, and enhance the resilience of the economy.
The Canadian economy is facing increasing challenges as trade tensions with the US show no signs of resolving, while global energy prices remain high due to conflict in the Middle East.
The combined pressures of tariffs, rising production costs, and inflation not only undermine growth prospects but also force Canada to adjust its development model, which is heavily reliant on the US market.
According to the Bank of Canada (BoC), the combination of trade uncertainty and high energy prices is making the economic outlook difficult to predict. In its September policy decision, the BoC kept its benchmark interest rate at 2.25% and warned that new US tariffs and Canada's retaliatory policies could affect the economic recovery.
In addition, high oil prices and the cost of refined energy products continue to put pressure on inflation in Canada. On October 14, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that the global diesel shortage could extend into 2027 due to conflicts disrupting supplies from the Middle East and Russia.
For Canada, one of the world's largest oil and gas producers and exporters, high energy prices have mixed effects. Oil and gas companies may benefit from higher selling prices, but transportation, manufacturing, agriculture , and consumers face increasingly high fuel costs. In particular, shortages of refined fuels could drive up domestic costs even though Canada possesses abundant crude oil reserves.
Responding to a Vietnam News Agency (VNA) reporter in Canada, Professor Vu Manh Chien, an economics expert at the University of Quebec, stated that trade developments in 2026 show that dependence on the US market is no longer simply a characteristic of the Canadian economy, but has become a strategic weakness.
According to the professor, by 2025, approximately 71.7% of Canada's exports will go to the US market, while Canada will only account for about 15.3% of US exports. This imbalance makes Canada more vulnerable when Washington changes its trade policies. In particular, the fact that 85.7% of Canadian export businesses sell to the US indicates that the risks are not concentrated only in large corporations but also extend to the network of small and medium-sized enterprises.
Professor Vu Manh Chien believes that tariff measures have not caused an immediate recession, but could weaken growth, reduce productivity, and cause businesses to delay investment. According to his calculations, the new tariff shock could reduce Canada's GDP by approximately 0.15-0.30% over 4 to 6 quarters, while around 15,000-35,000 jobs are at risk of being lost within a year, mainly in the woodworking, furniture, and automotive parts industries.
You may also like
A more concerning issue is the impact on long-term investment. Uncertainty in U.S. trade policy is causing businesses to reconsider expanding production capacity in Canada to serve the neighboring market. Even if some tariffs are lifted, investor confidence is unlikely to recover immediately.
Inflationary pressures are also presenting Canada's economic policy with a complex dilemma. The impact of US tariffs and Canada's retaliatory measures need to be clearly distinguished. While US import tariffs may reduce demand for Canadian goods, Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs directly drive up the prices of some imports and domestic production input costs.
Professor Vu Manh Chien estimates that the new round of tariffs could increase Canadian inflation by approximately 0.2-0.4 percentage points in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. Combined with high energy prices, this pressure could make it more difficult to bring inflation back to the Bank of Canada's 2% target.
According to the Bank of Canada (BoC), supply shocks such as soaring energy prices can both weaken economic activity and fuel inflation. This forces them to weigh the balance between supporting growth and maintaining price stability. Cutting interest rates too soon risks increasing inflation, while maintaining a tight monetary policy could create further difficulties for businesses and consumers.
However, Professor Vu Manh Chien argues that Canada still has significant advantages, particularly in the energy and strategic resources sectors. According to 2025 data from Canadian and US energy regulatory agencies, Canada exports approximately 4.3 million barrels of oil per day, of which about 3.9 million barrels go to the US. Canada also supplies the majority of imported crude oil and a significant proportion of natural gas and electricity to the US market.
The energy dependency is two-way, as many U.S. refineries are designed to use heavy oil from Canada. But the fact that 90% of Canada's crude oil exports go to the U.S. highlights the limitations of being able to redirect supply when trade relations become unstable.
Professor Vu Manh Chien argues that Canada should not use oil and gas as a tool for trade retaliation, as this risks harming the energy-producing provinces themselves and increasing tensions between the federal and local governments. Instead, Canada needs to expand its oil and gas transportation capacity to markets outside North America, develop its liquefied natural gas export base, and leverage its advantages in essential mineral resources.
You may also like
In the long term, market diversification is a necessary trade-off, even if Canada may have to accept some short-term growth costs. Developing export infrastructure, increasing domestic production capacity, and expanding trade relations with Europe and Asia will require significant time and capital.
Professor Vu Manh Chien particularly emphasized the need to remove trade barriers between Canadian provinces. According to him, this is one of the solutions that can create internal growth momentum, improve productivity, and reduce dependence on external fluctuations.
Against the backdrop of ongoing geopolitical conflicts driving up energy prices and unpredictable U.S. trade policies, the Canadian economy is facing a critical adjustment period. The ability to maintain price stability, protect jobs, and boost investment will depend not only on the outcome of negotiations with Washington but also on the speed of implementing reforms aimed at improving the competitiveness and resilience of the economy.

articles.title: APDA Webinar on Manufacturing in the Philippines: An Alternative for the Audio Industry - audioXpress
articles.summary: APDA Webinar on Manufacturing in the Philippines: An Alternative for the Audio Industry  audioXpress
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, the Audio Product Development Alliance (APDA) hosts a new live webinar on supply chain and manufacturing strategies. Sam Herec, CEO and Co-Founder of ASEAN Audio, will talk about the changing Asian manufacturing landscape and why the Philippines is becoming a real option for the audio industry. Learn from a Singapore-headquartered, Philippines-based ODM/OEM that works only on audio products and supports brands from concept to mass production.
Global technology brands keep adjusting to volatile US trade policy and a world that is realigning. Production is spreading across Southeast Asia, and the Philippines is getting more attention. The country has an established electronics and semiconductor manufacturing base, a skilled engineering and manufacturing workforce, and high English proficiency, which makes it easy for international customers to work there. It also has a mature export ecosystem built around the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) and good access to the wider Asian supply chain.
Sam Herec will give a balanced view of where the Philippines fits and where it doesn't. Which products and manufacturing models suit the country best? Where do China and other Asian manufacturing centers still have a clear advantage? And why does it make more sense to build a regional supply chain than to try to recreate Shenzhen in another country?
In this new live APDA session, Sam Herec will draw on his career in the audio industry and in Asian manufacturing to explain what led him to set up ASEAN Audio in the Philippines. He will also give his view on how manufacturing in Southeast Asia is changing. Why are more companies looking at a "China+1" strategy and other manufacturing locations? How do supply chain resilience, tariffs, geopolitics, and the need for more than one country of origin affect those decisions? And why doesn't moving final assembly mean taking China out of the supply chain?
The webinar will also look at the opportunity for the audio industry in particular. Consumer audio, installed AV, professional and MI products, and specialty electronics can all be a good fit, especially for low- and medium-volume production that combines product development, engineering, sourcing, and manufacturing under one roof. ASEAN Audio will serve as a case study: an audio-focused ODM/OEM/EMS model that uses Philippine manufacturing together with the wider Asian supplier ecosystem.
To close, Sam Herec will share how he expects manufacturing in Southeast Asia to develop over the next five to ten years, where the Philippines can become more competitive, and what that means for audio companies looking for alternatives. The main message is that the Philippines shouldn't be seen as a direct replacement for China. Instead, it is becoming a strong part of a more diversified Asian manufacturing strategy.
ASEAN Audio combines international management experience with Philippine engineering talent and a diversified regional supply chain. This webinar is also a rare chance to ask questions about the audio industry ecosystem in the region.

articles.title: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry - The Guardian
articles.summary: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry  The GuardianJudge Blocks Trump Administration’s Sanctions on 2 Groups Aiding the I.C.C.  The New York TimesU.S. Sanctions ICC in a Bid to Avoid “Criminal Liability”: War Crimes Prosecutor Reed Brody  Democracy Now!Nobel Peace Prize Winner Pillay Criticizes U.S. After Trump Rages About Losing Award  ForbesU.S. Court Blocks Enforcement of ICC Sanctions against Groups Advocating f...
articles.full_text:
A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza.
In a 30-page order issued on Tuesday, Jesse M Furman, a judge at the US district court for the southern district of New York, granted a preliminary injunction to the two groups, Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag).
The two organizations sued the Trump administration this summer, challenging an executive order issued in February 2025 that imposed sanctions against the ICC.
The order warned the US government would “impose tangible and significant consequences” on people involved in investigations that Washington said threatened the national security of the US or its allies, including Israel.
The order came after the ICC issued arrest warrants for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant, accusing them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Both men have rejected accusations against them, and the US government also opposed the court’s decision to issue the warrants.
In his opinion, Furman noted that last year two law professors brought a separate lawsuit challenging the 2025 executive order, and that the court had held that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny”.
Furman said that this lawsuit brought by Dawn and Taag – groups he described as “American advocacy organizations” – raised a “substantially similar challenge”. He wrote that the groups were challenging the 2025 order on “both statutory and constitutional grounds, re-upping many of the arguments made in the earlier cases”.
Dawn and Taag are rights groups that had worked to gather information for the ICC as it investigated allegations of war crimes against Palestinians.
“The court concludes that the 2025 order likely violates plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constitutes a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and cannot survive strict scrutiny,” Furman wrote.
However, the judge stopped short of declaring the executive order “facially unconstitutional” and rejected the groups’ request to “enjoin the president and to enter a ‘universal’ injunction barring enforcement of the 2025 order against anyone”.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on the ruling.
A spokesperson for the US state department said in a statement to the Guardian that “we do not comment on pending litigation” but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Joseph Pace, a lawyer for Dawn and Taag, described Tuesday’s decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”.
And in a statement, Omar Shakir, Dawn’s executive director, said: “Today, a US federal court has put the brakes in a major way on the Trump administration’s efforts to shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.”
Dawn also said that it would “immediately resume” its advocacy with the ICC “to prosecute Israeli and American perpetrators of grave crimes”.
The ruling comes just days after the US imposed financial sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: The Ministry of Industry and Trade updates its growth scenario, identifies targets and indicators, and assigns tasks for the fourth quarter of 2026. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Ministry of Industry and Trade updates its growth scenario, identifies targets and indicators, and assigns tasks for the fourth quarter of 2026.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Industry and Trade has just issued Official Letter No. 8293/BCT-KHTC dated October 12, 2026, to its affiliated units regarding updating growth scenarios, determining targets and indicators, and assigning tasks for the fourth quarter of 2026.
Accordingly, the update of the growth scenario aims to implement the tasks assigned in Government Resolution No. 01/NQ-CP dated January 8, 2026, on the main tasks and solutions for implementing the socio-economic development plan and state budget estimate for 2026; Decision No. 648/QD-BCT dated April 6, 2026, of the Minister of Industry and Trade on amending and supplementing the growth scenario of the Industry and Trade sector; and the conclusions of the Minister of Industry and Trade at the September briefing meeting on the implementation of tasks for the fourth quarter of 2026.
Six out of eight growth targets were met or exceeded after nine months.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade 's assessment, out of the 8 growth targets assigned by the Government , 6 have met or exceeded the planned targets, and 2 require focused attention in the fourth quarter of 2026.
By the end of September 2026, the industrial production index (IIP) is projected to increase by approximately 12.3%; total electricity production and imports will reach 266.58 billion kWh, an increase of approximately 9.65%; total power generation capacity will reach approximately 85,594.88 MW, an increase of approximately 3.57%; and the power generation capacity reserve ratio will reach approximately 25.97%.
Market and trade indicators continued to record growth. Exports increased by 24.5%; total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue increased by 13.4%; the B2C e-commerce market increased by 19.5%; and the percentage of businesses applying e-commerce reached 61%.
In September alone, exports reached $59.48 billion, a 39.1% increase compared to the same period last year; imports reached $58.21 billion, a 45.8% increase; and the trade surplus was $1.27 billion. For the first nine months of the year, exports totaled $434.3 billion, a 24.5% increase; imports totaled $453.7 billion, a 36.7% increase; and the trade balance showed a deficit of $19.4 billion.
However, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has identified two key indicators that need to be prioritized in the fourth quarter: total power generation capacity and growth in the B2C e-commerce market.
Specifically, the total power generation capacity is still short by approximately 2,570.12 MW compared to the minimum target of 88,165 MW by the end of the year. For the B2C e-commerce market, growth is still 0.5 percentage points lower than the lower end of the 20-22% target.
Manage on a monthly basis, proactively control risks.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade requires the identification of a single operational scenario: a scenario for achieving the 2026 targets, linked to a monthly timeline, including October, November, and December, instead of just monitoring results for the fourth quarter or the entire year.
Accordingly, the surplus achieved in the first nine months of 2026 constitutes a safe margin and should not be used to lower operating standards in the remaining months of the year.
You may also like
For indicators that have been significantly exceeded, such as exports, the focus should shift from accelerating growth at all costs to maintaining a reasonable growth rate, improving the quality of growth, controlling origin, trade risks, and the level of dependence on the FDI sector.
Regarding the Industrial Production Index (IIP), management should follow a safer and more feasible scenario, with contingency plans for risks arising from fluctuations in US tariff policies on key industrial exports, the trade deficit in the first nine months, and the impact of storms and floods in Central Vietnam. Simultaneously, clear responsibilities for monitoring and overseeing the IIP should be assigned to each industrial sector.
Another key requirement is risk-based management. Each indicator is linked to a risk forecast, a three-level warning threshold (Green, Yellow, Red) for each month, and a corresponding response scenario. When an indicator reaches the threshold, the lead unit must immediately activate the prepared solution, without waiting for the results of the entire quarter.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade also requested that resources be prioritized for management based on risk levels, with the Ministry's leadership focusing directly on two high-risk indicators: power generation capacity and B2C e-commerce, and two indicators with thin safety margins (IIP, total retail sales); the remaining indicators should be managed in a way that maintains the pace and improves the quality of growth.
Assign specific tasks to each unit, locality, and enterprise.
To implement the growth scenario for the fourth quarter of 2026, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has set monthly targets and assigned responsibilities to the relevant units for monitoring and implementation.
For the industrial production index, the target is to ensure the whole year remains within the 12-14% range, with an average increase of approximately 12.5-13.0% in the last months of the year. Total electricity production and imports in the fourth quarter are expected to be around 88.55 billion kWh; for the whole year, around 355.13 billion kWh, an increase of about 9.92%.
Total power generation capacity must reach a minimum of 88,165 MW by the end of the year; the power reserve ratio must be maintained at 21.8% or higher in every month. For exports, the annual growth target is 22.8% according to the updated target table. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue are expected to increase by approximately 13.3%; the B2C e-commerce market is expected to grow by approximately 20.5%; and the percentage of businesses applying e-commerce is expected to reach approximately 68%.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade assigns the lead units responsible for monitoring and achieving targets within their assigned functional scope and sector; and develops the Q4 action plan based on the principles of clear responsibilities, clear tasks, clear deadlines, clear products, and clear accountability for specific tasks.
Specifically, the Department of Industry is responsible for monitoring and compiling IIP indicators; the Department of Electricity coordinates with EVN, NSMO, and relevant units to monitor power sources and ensure electricity supply; the Department of Import and Export monitors export indicators; the Department of Domestic Market Management and Development monitors total retail sales; and the Department of E-commerce monitors the B2C e-commerce market and the percentage of businesses applying e-commerce.
For localities, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requires that localities with an IIP (Incremental Investment Performance Index) of less than 12% in the first nine months must allocate sufficient Q4 growth to compensate for the shortfall so that the annual target reaches at least 12%; localities with an IIP from 12% to less than 14% should strive for a growth rate no lower than 12.5% per month; and localities with an IIP of 14% or higher should maintain their growth rate and not lower the target.
Local authorities must also closely monitor export, retail, and e-commerce scenarios; for projects with a commercial operation (COD) milestone in the fourth quarter, monthly tasks must be assigned and responsible parties identified. The Department of Industry and Trade will monitor warning thresholds, promptly report to the Provincial/City People's Committee and the Ministry of Industry and Trade, along with compensation solutions, when indicators reach the Yellow or Red level; and simultaneously develop plans to respond to storms and floods, ensuring the maintenance of production, goods circulation, and electricity supply.
You may also like
For state-owned enterprises, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requires the implementation of commitments in the fourth quarter of 2026. EVN and NSMO are responsible for implementing their allocated electricity production, maintaining a reserve capacity of over 21.8%, ensuring the progress of power generation and grid projects, preparing contingency plans for storms and floods, and ensuring water storage in hydropower reservoirs for the 2027 dry season. PVN is responsible for ensuring the progress of power generation projects and supplying gas and LNG for power generation; TKV is responsible for ensuring coal production and the progress of projects under its management.
Relevant businesses must also ensure the production of fertilizers and chemicals, the supply of gasoline and diesel fuel, and maintain circulating reserves, preventing supply disruptions during the peak period at the end of the year.
Regarding implementation, the Ministry of Industry and Trade assigns Deputy Ministers to directly supervise units according to their assigned fields; the heads of these units are responsible to the Minister for the targets, tasks, quality, and progress of the assigned products.
The Planning and Finance Department is the central point for compiling and updating results monthly and reporting to the Ministry's leadership; the Ministry's Office coordinates in monitoring and expediting tasks that are behind schedule.
Departments of Industry and Trade, state-owned corporations and general companies are responsible for implementing assigned tasks, reporting immediately if there is a risk of not achieving targets, and contributing to ensuring the achievement of the industry and trade growth targets for 2026.

articles.title: SA factories crushed as Trump tariffs redirect Chinese goods - News24
articles.summary: SA factories crushed as Trump tariffs redirect Chinese goods  News24
articles.full_text:
- For more financial news, visit News24 Business.
South Africa’s manufacturing sector has been in decline for more than three decades. Now, a deluge of cheap Chinese goods, intensified by US President Donald Trump’s tariff war, is putting what remains of its industrial base under renewed pressure.
Chinese exports to South Africa have more than doubled since the start of the decade, rising by almost $10 billion (R165 billion) in the first eight months of this year compared with the same period six years ago. Among Africa’s major economies, only Nigeria recorded a bigger increase.
The pace has accelerated since Trump returned to the White House. Shipments from China to South Africa jumped 29% in the first eight months of 2026 from a year earlier, as Chinese manufacturers, confronting higher barriers in the US, hunt for customers elsewhere.
South Africa also runs a large trade deficit with China, which accounts for more than a third of the country’s manufacturing imports and only about 5.9% of exports, according to central bank data. The industry contracted for a third consecutive quarter in the three months through June.
Chinese manufacturers, aided by subsidies and a cheap currency, aren’t just undercutting producers in South Africa. Rivals from Brazil to Vietnam are also struggling to compete and have imposed tariffs on Chinese steel products. The European Union reached a deal with Beijing last week to curb Chinese hybrid-car exports to the bloc.
South Africa is particularly vulnerable as its manufacturers are already grappling with high energy costs, an inflexible labour market, burdensome regulation, failing infrastructure and weak economic growth.
The latest Manufacturing Vulnerability Index from Moody’s Ratings ranks Africa’s largest economy the most exposed to Chinese trade competition of the eight nations it assessed on the continent.
It attributed this to South Africa’s “relatively large manufacturing sector with a high reliance on foreign, and specifically Chinese, value added in exports” and moderate and declining competitiveness.
The International Trade Administration Commission, which administers trade laws and implements measures to protect local industries, said it is investigating five new applications from companies seeking relief from an influx of imports.
The applicants span sectors from producers of gypsum plasterboard, used for ceilings, to polyethylene terephthalate, a lightweight plastic used in beverage containers, to cold-rolled steel. The entities involved include the South African Fasteners Manufacturers’ Association, representing makers of steel nuts and bolts, Saint-Gobain Construction Products South Africa, ArcelorMittal South Africa, and Hosaf, a unit of KAP.
“Over the years, there has been a general increase in the case load relating to increased imports,” ITAC said in an emailed response to questions.
At Alvern Cables in Germiston, east of Johannesburg, works director Jaycen Padiachy has seen the impact of the influx of Chinese goods firsthand.
The company, which was founded in 1967 and produces low- and medium-voltage cables used in homes, factories and infrastructure, expected the rebound in economic activity after the global pandemic to help restore demand. Instead, Padiachy said, the recovery has faltered. “What we are noticing now is a lot of competition in the market; imports are affecting our business.”
To compete, the factory has had to adjust its business model. “Under recent market conditions, we’ve had to work on reduced time for a short period,” Padiachy said.
Wake-up call
Busi Mavuso, the head of Business Leadership South Africa, one of the country’s largest business lobby groups, apportions some of the blame for the influx of Chinese goods to the authorities.
“You don’t see the appetite from government to actually protect local industry, and yet they continue to talk about industrialisation and beneficiation,” she said in an interview. “The real fact of the matter is that we don’t have a clear trade policy as a country. We continue to put politics before economics, and that becomes concerning.”
The trade department says it is taking the threat seriously.
The upheaval in global trade is “a serious wake-up call,” Maoto Molefane, acting deputy director-general at the Department of Trade, said in an interview. “For the longest time, we’ve been dependent on a particular region, but going forward, South Africa is looking at other areas.”
The government wants companies to diversify their markets and is promoting a “butterfly strategy” aimed at strengthening trade links across different regions.
There is a paradox at the centre of South Africa’s industrial decline. The country hasn’t lost its ability to manufacture. Factory capacity utilisation stood at about 76% in 2026 from 83.2% in 2003, around levels seen in some major developed economies.
What it lacks is enough demand for goods priced at a level that will ensure its factories remain competitive, making investing in additional capacity difficult to justify.
South Africans are already under pressure from a high cost of living, unemployment and stagnant growth. When a cheaper imported alternative appears, price can outweigh arguments about supporting the local industry.
“Capability and capacity is not an issue,” Sello Takatso, senior manager for manufacturing at Nedbank Group, which lends to companies in the sector, said. “With the mounting challenges of imports that are taking place, we are competing on price point.”

articles.full_text:
In FocusThe China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
Chinese parts, machinery and know-how remain deeply embedded in countries seeking to build manufacturing industries of their own
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.
But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.
A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

articles.summary: Proposed tariff cuts welcomed by US firms  China Daily
articles.full_text:
Proposed tariff cuts welcomed by US firms
Business and industry representatives in the United States have welcomed the tariff reduction proposal on a total of $60 billion worth of goods put forward by the US-China Board of Trade in September, as the levies have caused uncertainty ahead of the holiday season.
The proposal to lower tariffs on both US and Chinese exports was announced by the Board of Trade on Sept 27, following President Xi Jinping's meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington, DC.
China's Ministry of Commerce said the US will reduce tariffs on imports from China including toys, home appliances, baby products, kitchen and bathroom fixtures and holiday gifts, while China will lower tariffs on imports from the US including agricultural products, personal care products, medical devices and coal.
In a statement, Greg Ahearn, president and CEO of The Toy Association, said: "The toy industry is pleased that toys have been designated as a category of nonsensitive goods under the US-China Board of Trade framework. This marks a historic win for American toy companies — 96 percent of which are small businesses and families — especially as we approach the holidays."
Gary C. Hufbauer, a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said that if the tariff reductions proposed by the Board of Trade materialize, they could lead to "significant gains" for both sides.
However, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer recently stated that no timeline has been decided to cut tariffs on goods recommended by the Board of Trade.
"We have to stick to our legal processes," he told the G20 trade ministers' meeting that took place from Sept 30 to Oct 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
He added that other USTR Section 301 investigations into Chinese products would continue.
In another significant move, the US and China extended an agreement to pause imposition of higher tariffs by two months — it was set to expire on Nov 10.
While the pause provides temporary clarity for US businesses, many still want a long-term solution to steady the US-China trade relationship further, said an expert.
Professor Wei Liang, the Gordon Paul Smith Chair of international policy at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey in California, said that uncertainty over the length of future tariff pauses hits not only US companies that invest in China, but also other companies that want to continue to manufacture in China and then export back to the US market.
"They cannot just rely on this (pause of) six months, 10 months, 12 months, tariffs. They really need a clear message before they know what to do next. That market uncertainty has hurt a lot of business interests," she said.
Meanwhile, according to a survey by China Beige Book, a research firm based in New York, US businesses have placed more orders for Chinese goods this year than a year ago.
Its survey, seen by CNBC, found that as "China's relative tariff position improved", shipments to the US rose on both a yearly and monthly basis, according to the data taken from a poll of 1,295 Chinese companies from Sept 1 to 22.

articles.title: Piyush Goyal sees India becoming global car manufacturing hub as demand grows - CNBC TV18
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal sees India becoming global car manufacturing hub as demand grows  CNBC TV18
articles.full_text:
Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal stated that India is poised to become a global car manufacturing hub as growing demand makes local production viable. He noted that trade deals protect the mass-market vehicle segment while luxury carmakers expand operations.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has expressed confidence that India could emerge as a global car manufacturing hub as demand grows enough to make local production commercially viable for international automakers.
Speaking at the ‘Dilli Dialogue: Policies for a Future-Ready India’ in New Delhi, Goyal said the import quotas permitted under India’s trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the European Union largely cover expensive cars, while the mass-market segment for vehicles priced below ₹17 lakh remains protected.
He cited luxury carmakers setting up manufacturing plants in Pune after initially testing the Indian market as an example of how international manufacturers could expand production in India as demand grows.
Goyal also said European Union regulations could make car manufacturing in the bloc less competitive and encourage companies to shift more production to India.
“Tatas had so much trouble after they bought Jaguar. Tata Motors itself was going to collapse and then they put in a lot of re-engineering, and shift some models to India. Finally they were able to make money after years,” he said.
Electronics, tourism and jobs
Goyal said India needed a two-pronged approach: adopting the world's best technologies while identifying sectors with significant potential to create jobs and businesses.
He pointed to rising demand for electronics and white goods as an opportunity to attract investment into domestic manufacturing, including semiconductor fabrication plants.
Tourism, he said, was another sector with considerable potential to generate employment and create new business opportunities. Artificial intelligence could make tourism promotion more efficient, but human experiences would remain central to the industry.
“AI can only add to the efficiency of promoting tourism. But otherwise, human experiences will always be AI proof,” he said.
India’s workforce and trade strategy
Highlighting India's demographic advantage, Goyal referred to demand for Indian workers in countries such as Germany and Japan. He said people from the North-East could serve as India's brand ambassadors in nursing and caregiving, while describing the region as a gateway to ASEAN and the Far East.
Goyal said he had participated in 10 bilateral meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in the US last month. He added that he was scheduled to meet ministers from the UK and Canada in New Delhi on October 12 and 13, respectively.
He also criticised trade decisions taken by the previous United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, referring to a Cabinet resolution on Vietnam's market-economy status and free trade agreements involving the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) and ASEAN.
Goyal said India had trade agreements with Australia, New Zealand, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and the European Union that excluded dairy products to protect the interests of small farmers.
He added that he did not believe other trade ministers viewed politeness as a sign of weakness.

articles.title: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next - Fortune
articles.summary: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next  Fortune
articles.full_text:
Thai real estate developer Amata Corporation says Laos will become its “largest focus” in the years to come, CEO Vikrom Kromadit tells Fortune.
“Laos will become our largest focus because of the land bank that they have,” Kromadit tells Fortune. “They also have lots of green energy—that’s why they’re called the battery of Southeast Asia.”
Amata expanded into Laos in 2022, starting with Amata City Namor, which covers 31.5 square kilometers and sits beside a station on the China-Laos Railway. The company says its long-term Laos vision could reach 200 square kilometers.
Kromadit’s company built its fortunes in Thailand and Vietnam. Amata Corporation, founded in 1989, built industrial parks across Thailand’s Rayong and Chon Buri provinces. It was also an early backer of Vietnam, building its first facility there in 1994, early in the Southeast Asian country’s reform program. Laos, however, offers an opportunity for Amata to capture Chinese manufacturers expanding to new manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia.
Laos, Southeast Asia’s only landlocked country, boasts a huge energy surplus, as its rivers and mountainous terrain supported a government-led push to build hydroelectric dams as a core economic pillar. The country currently exports about 80% of its electricity to other Asian countries like Thailand, China, and Singapore.
“They have plenty of land and a lot of water,” Kromadit says, adding that it has “the best natural conditions” for industrial development. (While Laos generates over 12 GW of capacity from over 80 hydro plants, most cross-border transmission lines bypass local communities, sticking consumers with frequent blackouts.)
To Kromadit, Laos’s potential is also backed by China, long the country’s top foreign investor. In 2025, China pumped $18 billion into Laos’s economy, primarily toward industry, mining, and agriculture, according to the Vientiane Times, a local newspaper.
Laos has been slotted into “China plus one” supply chains, where both Chinese and global manufacturers move some—or all—of their production to other countries, both to reduce cost and avoid tariffs on Chinese-origin products.
“China is the largest manufacturer of all products, so they can’t just keep building only within their country,” Kromadit explains. “They’re also being hit by political pressure from the U.S.”
After graduating from National Taiwan University with a degree in mechanical engineering, he returned to Thailand in 1975 and founded V&K Enterprise, an import-export business that focused on agricultural products, minerals, and seafood. But by the 1980s, he was frustrated with being “just a middleman.”
“I wanted to make more money,” Kromadit confesses. “When I was in the food business, even though I was the one who created all the channels and brought in business, once companies achieved success, they kicked me out.”
In 1988, he cofounded the Bang Pakong Industrial Estate on the eastern coast of Bangkok, then established Amata Corporation in 1989. Amata’s first industrial facility, Amata City Chon Buri, opened that same year.
After Kromadit visited Vietnam in 1990, he decided to make the country Amata’s first overseas market. “I found that the Vietnamese were focused, capable, and smart,” he says. “I thought that Vietnam, in the future, would compete with Thailand for industrial investments.” Amata launched Amata City Bien Hoa in Dong Nai province in 1994.
His prediction has largely come true: Vietnam is now Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economy, with Q3 GDP growth of 9.95%. Hanoi wants to have Vietnam reach high-income status by 2045.
Amata today hosts more than 1,500 factories in 12 locations across Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos. It briefly attempted an expansion into Myanmar in 2019, with a facility in Yangon, the country’s commercial center. Plans were halted in early 2021 following a military coup and resulting civil war.
Amata positions its facilities as industrial cities that include not just factories but also housing, schools, hospitals, and shopping malls. The company’s flagship Chon Buri campus, for instance, houses the massive 38,000-square-meter Lotus Plus Mall, which includes a hypermarket, retail stores, banks, restaurants, and an international cinema.
The company’s facilities include kindergartens, schools, and technical training institutes, with more on the way. “We’re now looking to build a university,” Kromadit says.
Asked whether Amata might expand into other Southeast Asian markets, like Indonesia or Cambodia, Kromadit says the company already has enough land to occupy him for the rest of his life.
“The land that we have on hand is around 700 square kilometers,” he says. “It’s big enough to make me busy until I go to heaven.”
