AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that producers/exporters subject to this review made sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to 15 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.
DATES:
Applicable October 15, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Walter Ankner or T.J. Worthington, AD/CVD Operations, Office III, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-8374 or (202) 482-4567, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 22, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on certain pasta (pasta) from Italy.[1]
On September 24, 2025, Commerce selected La Molisana, S.p.A. (La Molisana) and Pastificio Lucio Garofalo S.p.A. (Garofalo) as the mandatory respondents in this review.[2]
On September 3, 2025, La Doria Pasta PL S.r.l. (La Doria) timely withdrew its request for review.[3]
On October 28, 2025, 8th Avenue Food & Provisions, Inc. and Winland Foods, Inc. (collectively, the domestic interested parties) timely withdrew their request for review of 17 companies.[4]
On October 29, 2025, Pastificio Di Martino Gaetano e Flli S.p.A. (Di Martino) timely withdrew its request for review.[5]
On November 10, 2025, Marchesi Frescobaldi Soc. Agricola S.r.l. (Frescobaldi) timely withdrew its request for review.[6]
On January 27, 2026, Barilla America Inc. and Barilla G. e R. Fratelli Società per Azioni Socio Unico (collectively, Barilla) timely withdrew their request for review.[7]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as Appendix I of this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise subject to the
Order
is pasta from Italy. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if a party who requested a review withdraws its request within 90 days of the date of publication of notice of initiation. As noted above, Commerce received timely-filed withdrawal requests with respect to the companies listed in Appendix III, and no other parties requested an administrative review of these companies. Therefore, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to these companies, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) and (2) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Export price and constructed export price are calculated in accordance with section 772 of the Act. NV is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rate for Non-Individually Examined Companies
The Act and Commerce's regulations do not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(c)(2) of the Act. Generally, Commerce looks to section 735(c)(5) of the Act, which provides instructions for calculating the all-others rate in a market economy investigation, for guidance when calculating the rate for companies which were not selected for individual examination in an administrative review.
Under section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act, the all-others rate is normally an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any rates that are zero,
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.5 percent), or determined entirely on the basis of facts available. Where the weighted-average dumping margin for each of the individually examined companies is zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available, section 735(c)(5)(B) of the Act provides that Commerce may use “any reasonable method to establish the estimated all-others rate for exporters and producers
( printed page 65526)
not individually investigated, including averaging the estimated weighted-average dumping margins determined for the exporters and producers individually investigated.”
In this administrative review, we preliminarily calculated weighted-average dumping margins for the mandatory respondents, La Molisana and Garofalo, that are not zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available. Accordingly, we are preliminarily assigning to the companies under review that were not selected for individual examination a weighted-average dumping margin equal to the simple average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins calculated for La Molisana and Garofalo, consistent with 19 CFR 351.109(g).[9]

articles.title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone off Alaska; Pacific Ocean Perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska
articles.summary: NMFS is prohibiting retention of the incidental catch allowance for Pacific Ocean perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) except by vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. This action is necessary because the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) apportioned as the incidental catch allowance for Pacific Ocean perch in the Central GOA will soon be or has been reached.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
                    SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting retention of the incidental catch allowance for Pacific Ocean perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) except by vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. This action is necessary because the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) apportioned as the incidental catch allowance for Pacific Ocean perch in the Central GOA will soon be or has been reached.
                    DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 14, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The 2026 Pacific Ocean perch TAC apportioned as the incidental catch allowance in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit is 2,800 metric tons as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish of the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the 2026 TAC of Pacific Ocean perch apportioned as the incidental catch allowance for vessels other than vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit will soon be or has been reached.
Therefore, in accordance with § 679.
20(d)(2), NMFS is prohibiting retention of the incidental catch allowance for Pacific Ocean perch for vessels in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA other than vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit and requiring that Pacific ocean perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA be treated in the same manner as a prohibited species, as described under § 679.
21(a), for the remainder of the year, except for Pacific Ocean perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA caught by catcher vessels using hook-and-line, pot, or jig gear as described in § 679.
20(j), or caught by catcher vessels using trawl gear participating in the electronic monitoring program as described in § 679.
21(a)(2).
This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 Pacific Ocean perch TAC apportioned as the incidental catch allowance in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
This action does not apply to vessels checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit.
While this prohibition is effective the requirements of § 679.
20(j)(4) apply.

Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data in a timely fashion and would delay prohibiting the retention of Pacific Ocean perch apportioned as the incidental catch allowance in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on the total catch of Pacific Ocean perch in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 13, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.
                    
                    
                        16 U.S.C. 1801 
                        et seq.
                
                    Dated: October 13, 2026.

articles.full_text:
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice; receipt of application for Letter of Authorization; request for comments and information.
SUMMARY:
NMFS has received a request from the Sonoma County Water Agency (SCWA) for authorization to take small numbers of marine mammals incidental to Russian River Estuary management activities in Sonoma County, California over the course of five years from the date of issuance. Pursuant to regulations implementing the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), NMFS is announcing receipt of the SCWA's request for the development and implementation of regulations governing the incidental taking of marine mammals. NMFS invites the public to provide information, suggestions, and comments on the SCWA's application and request.
DATES:
Comments and information must be received no later than November 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments on the applications should be addressed to the Permits and Conservation Division, Office of Protected Resources, National Marine Fisheries Service. Physical comments should be sent to 1315 East-West Highway, Silver Spring, MD 20910 and electronic comments should be sent to
ITP.cockrell@noaa.gov.
Instructions:
NMFS is not responsible for comments sent by any other method, to any other address or individual, or received after the end of the comment period. Comments received electronically, including all attachments, must not exceed a 25-megabyte file size. Attachments to electronic comments will be accepted in Microsoft Word or Excel or Adobe PDF file formats only. All comments received are a part of the public record and will generally be posted online at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/marine-mammal-protection/incidental-take-authorizations-construction-activities
without change. All personal identifying information (
e.g., name, address) voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do not submit confidential business information or otherwise sensitive or protected information.
Craig Cockrell, Office of Protected Resources, NMFS, (301) 427-8401.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Sections 101(a)(5)(A) and (D) of the MMPA (16 U.S.C. 1361et seq.) direct the Secretary of Commerce (as delegated to NMFS) to allow, upon request, the incidental, but not intentional, taking of small numbers of marine mammals by U.S. citizens who engage in a specified activity (other than commercial fishing) within a specified geographical region if certain findings are made and either regulations are issued or, if the taking is
( printed page 65532)
limited to harassment, a notice of a proposed authorization is provided to the public for review.
An incidental take authorization shall be granted if NMFS finds that the taking will have a negligible impact on the species or stock(s), will not have an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of the species or stock(s) for subsistence uses (where relevant), and if the permissible methods of taking and requirements pertaining to the mitigation, monitoring and reporting of such takings are set forth.
NMFS has defined “negligible impact” in 50 CFR 216.103 as an impact resulting from the specified activity that cannot be reasonably expected to, and is not reasonably likely to, adversely affect the species or stock through effects on annual rates of recruitment or survival.
The MMPA states that the term “take” means to harass, hunt, capture, kill or attempt to harass, hunt, capture, or kill any marine mammal.
Except with respect to certain activities not pertinent here, the MMPA defines “harassment” as: any act of pursuit, torment, or annoyance, which (i) has the potential to injure a marine mammal or marine mammal stock in the wild (Level A harassment); or (ii) has the potential to disturb a marine mammal or marine mammal stock in the wild by causing disruption of behavioral patterns, including, but not limited to, migration, breathing, nursing, breeding, feeding, or sheltering (Level B harassment).
Summary of Request
On July 1, 2026, NMFS received application from the SCWA requesting authorization for take of marine mammals incidental to Russian River Estuary management activities in Sonoma County, California. After the SCWA responded to our questions and revised the application on August 27, 2026, we determined the application was adequate and complete on October 7, 2026. The requested regulations would be valid for five years (2027-2032). The proposed action requires the use of heavy equipment (
e.g., bulldozer and excavator) and increased human presence, as well as the use of small boats. As a result, pinnipeds hauled out on the beach or at peripheral haul-outs in the estuary may exhibit behavioral responses that indicate incidental take by Level B harassment under the MMPA. Therefore, the SCWA requests authorization to incidentally take marine mammals.
The SCWA plans to continue managing the naturally-formed barrier beach at the mouth of the Russian River in order to minimize potential for flooding adjacent to the estuary and to enhance habitat for juvenile salmonids, as well as to conduct biological and physical monitoring of the barrier beach and estuary. Artificial breaching and monitoring activities may occur at any time during the period of validity of the proposed regulations.
Information Solicited
Interested persons may submit information, suggestions, and comments concerning the SCWA's request (see
ADDRESSES
). NMFS will consider all information, suggestions, and comments related to the request during the development of proposed regulations governing the incidental taking of marine mammals by the SCWA, if appropriate.
Dated: October 13, 2026.
Kimberly Damon-Randall,
Director, Office of Protected Resources, National Marine Fisheries Service.

articles.title: America Didn’t Lose Its Rare Earth Industry. It Sold It. - Lawfare
articles.summary: America Didn’t Lose Its Rare Earth Industry. It Sold It.  LawfareMonazite Is the Radioactive Ore That Could Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths  Foreign PolicyWhat a Radioactive Lake In China Can Teach the World About Rare Earths  IEEE SpectrumChina’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs MagazineCan the USA Take on China's Rare Earth Dominance? | Expert Webinar  Off Grid Energy Indep...
articles.full_text:
In October 2025, Beijing imposed sweeping controls on its rare earth exports. Since then, those controls have been suspended one short reprieve at a time, in the latest instance until Nov. 10, with a broader trade truce through Jan. 10, 2027. The reprieves have repeatedly come only after American concessions, demonstrating China’s leverage in the export fight.
Yet China has constricted sales even during the truce, as buyers have few options but to take what they can get. In June, with the suspension in force, Beijing placed MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, the two companies the U.S. is counting on to build an alternative supply to China, on an export control list.
Washington’s effort to rebuild the supply chain, meanwhile, has not yet reached the scale or durability the problem requires. With up to $100 billion in loan authority specifically earmarked for critical minerals in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the capital undoubtedly exists. What is missing is alignment of interests among the parties that would supply and benefit from it, and a political system patient enough to hold a course for the decade or more that rebuilding a supply chain takes.
This article’s authors work at the intersection of finance and national security. Between the three of us, we have watched the same on-again, off-again rhythm play out in both Chinese statecraft and U.S. budget fights. A consistent pattern plays out: Capital markets are good at financing efficient supply but are not good at financing a binary outcome, such as insurance against a monopoly state seller that can manipulate both price and availability. And subsidies alone will not close that gap. We have seen firsthand that what the U.S. government has to offer right now insufficiently incentivizes private investors, because its tools are market tools deployed in an environment of market failure. Instead, we propose a financing instrument that could clear both economic and political hurdles: a contingent convertible security that converts into ownership if Beijing weaponizes supply.
Rare Earths Are a Market Failure
The history of how we got here is well known, but worth retelling briefly. The Chinese Communist Party inherited its strategic focus on building industrial capacity from the Soviet Union. In 1964, Deng Xiaoping inspected an iron ore mine near the Mongolian border holding the world’s largest rare earth deposit. He ordered the engineers to develop steel and rare earths alike. Since then, as technologies have increasingly relied on specialized materials, the Chinese Communist Party under successive leaders has deliberately invested in and consolidated control over the rare earths industry. China refines more than 90 percent of the world’s rare earths and close to 99 percent of heavy rare earths today. It processes nearly all the heavy elements that go into precision-guided weapons and advanced chips.
When Beijing tightened export controls in October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized it as “pointing a bazooka at the supply chains and industrial base of the entire free world.” Remarkably, the entire market for rare earth oxides is worth less than $10 billion. That a $10 billion market can grind to a halt trillions in global gross domestic product is the definition of a chokepoint. Beijing controls this chokepoint today by design. Decades of state policy work laid the groundwork for the Chinese Communist Party to enact an international licensing system by 2025. General Secretary Xi Jinping himself openly speaks about the importance of maintaining global dependency on China’s industrial supply chains.
Hindsight treats this as neglect, something policymakers lost sight of and let slip during the U.S.’s unipolar moment. That is a necessary, but only partial, explanation. The truth is the United States did not lose its rare earth industry due to carelessness. Private American companies willingly sold it, for reasons that made perfect economic sense at the time and still do. China bought it for reasons that were never purely economic. That mismatch explains why, after years of investment and policy attention, the dependency remains.
Until the late 1980s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and refiner of rare earths. But it was a dirty business: The Mountain Pass mine in California leaked roughly 600,000 gallons of radioactive and other waste into the Mojave. As cleanup and regulatory costs mounted and profits fell, the mine shut down in stages starting in the 1990s until it was fully idle by 2002. Meanwhile, the work moved to China, where the state subsidized unprofitable operations, tolerated pollution, and sold the processed oxides back to the U.S. at rock-bottom prices.
The same thing happened to the magnets: In 1995, General Motors sold Magnequench, its magnet unit, to a Chinese-backed consortium. By 2006, the last U.S. plant had closed, and the machine tools and equipment had been shipped to China. Economists would say this was the right move for a free market economy. Comparative advantage did what it was supposed to do, and a dirty, low-margin business left a wealthy country for a developing one. There was even a strategic rationale: Drawing China into the trading system, the wishful thinking went, would also make it a responsible stakeholder rather than a rival.
The category error was to conceive rare earths as a market, rather than recognizing it as a geostrategic industry. A market solves for the lowest cost. To be sure, Chinese producers competed on cost, and they rode a tech boom with surging demand for their product. But a state will pay almost any price to control a chokepoint, because tolerating a money-losing business pales in comparison to the geopolitical leverage that it brings. Over time, China has become less market driven, not more. Meanwhile, the U.S. continued to treat as a market what the Chinese Communist Party came to appreciate as a strategic program.
Control over the chokepoint gives Beijing a switch. When it lets the material flow, no private interest will build alternative supply chains at scale, because Chinese state-funded producers can sell at or below cost indefinitely, and no rational private investor will willingly sign up to lose money. When China cuts off the flow, the incentives reverse overnight, but capacity cannot follow overnight, because standing up the full supply chain and rebuilding the lost know-how can take a decade or longer.
This is classic market failure in which the same critical material can become worthless or priceless on command. In 2010, during a maritime dispute with Japan, Beijing reportedly halted rare earth shipments, and Tokyo quickly conceded. The short-term truces of the past year, each struck around contentious but episodic trade disputes, further entrench that market failure. Each successive loosening and tightening seems designed to keep the United States and its allies off balance and frustrate any long-term plan to reduce Beijing’s leverage.
Government Money Has to Survive Politics
If the market will not rebuild the rare earths supply chain, the government must do so.
Administrations under both parties have tried, and their attempts have run into a predictable morass of misaligned interests. The parties to government financing all want different things. Private investors want attractive returns in fat years, while having the government carry losses in lean ones. Commercial lenders want years of fully contracted offtake to guarantee interest payments, while Congress typically appropriates money for the next year. Markets want flexibility while Congress wants tight oversight and guardrails. Washington often wants to be the last (and lightest) money in, which signals to investors that the government is hedging. And cheap, open-ended financing is exactly the wrong signal to send to management teams.
The Pentagon’s latest playbook acknowledges that the market, left to its own devices, simply will not finance uneconomic redundancy. As a result, the July 2025 deal with MP Materials includes $400 million in convertible preferred stock, loans, equity warrants, a 10-year guaranteed price floor, and a 10-year offtake commitment. The deal was right for its moment, as it gets the producer going and sustains it while Beijing floods the market. But the deal blurs two different roles: In ordinary years, the government is a lender, financing capacity the market will not; in a crisis, it has insured against a geopolitical event. These two roles call for two different return profiles. Because the deal does not separate them, it puts the government in the unenviable position of simultaneously absorbing losses and inviting the charge of nationalization, all without a clear exit strategy.
Without some structure to navigate potentially painful political costs, these financing arrangements will come under pressure during budget cycles and electoral turnover. And that is simply untenable, because when it comes to the decade-plus timeline to stand up a rare earths supply chain, whatever Washington builds must outlast the administration that built it.
A Financial Instrument That Responds to Beijing’s Behavior
Our proposal is a financial instrument that aligns these interests. In financial parlance, the instrument is called a contingent convertible security, also known as a CoCo bond, issued by the producer to the government and any private lenders who wish to join, paired with guaranteed offtake at a price floor. Its form changes with two externally observable conditions: the producer’s capacity build-out and Beijing’s behavior.
Here’s how it works. In its starting form (and in quiet years), a CoCo bond is a simple loan paying interest. Two triggers change its form. The first is capacity. The producer must cross a defined capacity threshold by a fixed date. Capacity can be measured as units of output in mining, refining, or manufacturing critical minerals. articles.title: Expert: Global supply chains remain interconnected despite trade tensions - China Daily
articles.summary: Expert: Global supply chains remain interconnected despite trade tensions  China Daily
articles.full_text:
From chocolate chips and computer chips to athletic shoes and frozen fish, everyday products consumed by Americans often travel through complex international supply networks before reaching store shelves and households.
In his forthcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Strange Economic Power of Global Supply Chains, Willy Shih, a professor of management practice in business administration at Harvard Business School, explores the intricate connections behind global manufacturing and trade, and why understanding those connections matters in an increasingly uncertain economic environment.
Speaking at a virtual media briefing hosted by the Port of Los Angeles on Friday, Shih said his motivation for writing the book grew out of a realization that many people have little understanding of where the products they purchase actually originate.
Recalling his conversations with students, Shih said many simply assumed that products came from online retailers such as Amazon, without considering the extensive manufacturing and transportation networks involved.
"What I really want to do is I want the world to have a better understanding of where their stuff comes from, how interconnected we are," he said.
Drawing on 28 years of industry experience, Shih said he had witnessed China's opening to the world and the transformation of global manufacturing. As businesses reassess their supply chains amid tariffs, geopolitical uncertainty and shifting trade policies, he emphasized that deeply integrated production networks linking China with the US and other economies remain difficult to replace, despite efforts to diversify manufacturing and sourcing away from China.
Responding to a question from China Daily about whether the recent China-US summit and extended trade truce could bring greater stability and predictability to global businesses, Shih said companies were increasingly seeking flexibility in their sourcing strategies.
"I think companies are now trying to create more optionality and diversify some of their risk," he said. "With that uncertainty hanging over people, it's very hard to make long-term decisions and long-term commitments."
While companies are encouraging suppliers to diversify production, Shih said the process of restructuring global supply chains is complicated.
"Until we get some kind of longer-term stability, I don't think we're going to be settling into new patterns. So I think being agile is going to be the new normal."
Discussing the "China Plus One" strategy, under which companies diversify manufacturing and sourcing beyond China while maintaining operations there, Shih said shifting final assembly to other countries does not necessarily reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers.
Although China's direct share of US imports has declined significantly since 2017, he said Chinese components continue to play an important role in countries such as Vietnam and Mexico.
"Companies, in some sense, are rearranging the final assembly step while the upstream dependence remains," Shih said.
Shih pointed to new shipping connections between Chinese ports, including Shanghai and Ningbo, and Mexico's Pacific coast as evidence of how supply chains are being reorganized rather than simply severed.
He explained that manufacturers moving assembly operations often continue importing intermediate goods from China because established supplier networks offer specialized capabilities and competitive costs.
Building alternative supply chains requires substantial time and investment, he said, recalling how China gradually developed its own manufacturing ecosystem after initially relying heavily on imported components.
"Now if we're talking about localizing supply chains to Mexico, that'll take a decade. That's not something that happens overnight," Shih said.
Shih also questioned whether tariffs alone could bring large-scale manufacturing back to the US.
He said American manufacturers remain competitive in advanced industries requiring specialized technology and proprietary expertise, but the economics of producing many labor-intensive consumer goods domestically remain challenging.
"We should not be afraid to import components or specialized materials from people who can do it better than us as well," he said.
For Shih, the challenges facing global commerce reinforce the central message of his book: international production networks are deeply interconnected, and their benefits are often overlooked.
He cited examples such as frozen fish processed in Qingdao, China, before being shipped to Los Angeles in refrigerated containers, illustrating how products routinely cross borders through specialized manufacturing and logistics networks.
He said understanding how these networks operate could help businesses, policymakers and consumers better appreciate the economic relationships that support everyday life.
"The more the world understands not only the interconnectedness, but the benefits that we get from that interconnectedness and interdependency, the more people understand that, I think the better off we all are," Shih said.
As the Port of Los Angeles reported record cargo volumes, its executive director Gene Seroka said it underscores the resilience of international trade despite policy uncertainty.
"For now, purchase orders back in Asia remain solid, and our customers are moving that cargo when the opportunity is there," Seroka said.

articles.title: japan-india-fdi-2026 - Spherical Insights
articles.summary: japan-india-fdi-2026  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
Japan became India’s largest source of foreign direct investment in early FY2026–27, driven largely by MUFG’s investment in Shriram Finance. Growing activity in automobiles, semiconductors, clean energy, and finance signals broader cooperation. However, regulatory hurdles and uneven investment flows could affect future growth.
Japan Becomes India’s Largest FDI Source as Quarterly Inflows Top $5.7 Billion
Government data from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) show that Japan invested $5.71 billion in India in the April-June 2026 quarter, ranking first ahead of Singapore at $5.22 billion and Mauritius at about $2.4 billion. The figure is higher than the $3.74 billion Japan invested in all of FY26 and the $2.48 billion in FY25. Japan supplied nearly 29% of India’s total equity FDI of $19.81 billion, which rose 6% from $18.62 billion a year earlier.
One transaction dominates the number. MUFG Bank completed the purchase of a 20% stake in Shriram Finance for ₹39,618 crore (about $4.4 billion) in April, one of the largest cross-border investments in India’s financial services sector. On reported figures that is roughly three-quarters of Japan’s quarterly total. An equity partner at Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas said large strategic deals drove the headline, while Japanese expansion plans point to a deeper long-term opportunity in manufacturing, financial services, and technology.
The mix of investors also shifted. FDI from the United States fell about 76% to $1.34 billion, and inflows were uneven within the quarter, slowing after a strong April. That contrast has increased attention on Japan as a stable, long-horizon source of capital.
Policy support is strong. At the 15th annual summit in August 2025, the two governments set a ¥10 trillion (about $67 billion) target for Japanese private investment in India over a decade. During Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s visit in July 2026, Japanese firms announced investments of about $12.5 billion (roughly ₹1 trillion), and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said around ₹1 lakh crore of the target has already been invested.
India Equity FDI USD 19.81 Billion in Q1 FY27, up 6% from USD 18.62 Billion a year earlier, with Japan contributing USD 5.71 Billion, or nearly 29%.
Why Is Japanese Capital Flowing Into India Now?
Several factors explain the timing.
First, supply-chain diversification. Deloitte India’s Anil Talreja says Japan is diversifying supply chains because of geopolitical tensions and rising costs, and industry experts also cite tariff risks.
Second, strong earnings from India. In a JETRO survey, 78.7% of Japanese companies reporting higher profits credited rising Indian demand, and 62.5% of Japanese automotive-related firms in India expected higher operating profit in 2026, the highest share among major markets surveyed.
Third, policy and infrastructure. India has set up 12 Japanese industrial townships across nine states, and both governments are working under an economic-security agenda covering semiconductors, clean energy, pharmaceuticals, and critical minerals. A July 2026 joint statement added AI cooperation covering data centers and computing capacity.
Finally, financial services. Japanese banks and institutions are expanding in lending, banking, insurance, and investment services, with MUFG and SMBC making some of the largest announced commitments.
Ready to lead the Japan-India FDI 2026?
Discover the regional trends and growth factors shaping the industry. We’re here to assist with expert, personalized data.
Call +1 303 800 4326 or Send us a message for a personalized consultation.
Market statistics
- Japan invested $5.71 billion in India in April–June 2026, about 29% of the quarter’s $19.81 billion equity FDI, and more than its full-year totals of $3.74 billion (FY26) and $2.48 billion (FY25).
- Singapore ranked second with $5.22 billion, while US inflows fell about 76% to $1.34 billion.
- Japan’s cumulative FDI into India was $48.14 billion from April 2000 to March 2026, about 6% of the total and fifth-largest overall, with more than 1,400 Japanese companies operating in India.
- Bilateral trade reached about $27.5 billion in FY2025-26, and the two countries are reviewing the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
- Japan’s private investment target is ¥10 trillion (~$67 billion) over ten years, and firms announced about $12.5 billion during the July 2026 summit.
Major Developments Shaping Japan-India Investment in 2026
- Japan Tops India’s FDI Table in April–June 2026
Japan’s $5.71 billion quarterly inflow is close to the best single-year total in India’s 25-year record for Japanese FDI, according to commentary from NITI Aayog officials, and marks a shift from occasional deal-led spikes toward a broader build-up of manufacturing and technology capital.
- MUFG Completes a 20% Stake in Shriram Finance
MUFG Bank’s ₹39,618 crore (about $4.4 billion) investment, completed in April, is the main reason for Japan’s lead. SMBC’s partnership with Yes Bank, valued at about ₹170 billion, adds to Japanese bank commitments.
- The July 2026 Summit Delivers About ₹1 Trillion in Announcements
During Prime Minister Takaichi’s three-day visit, more than 150 Japanese companies joined the Japan-India Economic Forum and firms announced about $12.5 billion across roughly 120 deals. Suzuki committed ₹50 billion for land and a new plant, Toyota plans a 100,000-vehicle-a-year facility at Bidkin, Daikin is building a ₹10 billion R&D center in Haryana, and Sumitomo announced a ₹38 billion collaboration. The leaders also opened Maruti Suzuki’s fourth plant at Kharkhoda.
- Goyal Leads India’s Largest Business Delegation to Japan
In August 2026, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal took more than 200 business leaders to Tokyo, Nagoya, and Osaka, met over 30 Japanese institutions including MUFG, Mizuho, and Nomura, and chaired a semiconductor and AI roundtable. He committed to a framework to ease compliance, including BIS certification, for high-technology factories.
- Semiconductor Projects Move Toward Production
Renesas has invested in CG Power’s chip assembly and test project in Gujarat, with mass production due to begin in 2026, and Tokyo Electron is working with Tata Electronics and plans a presence at Dholera.
What Challenges Could Limit the Momentum?
The headline is strong, but the underlying picture has risks.
- Deal-Driven Concentration: One financial transaction makes up most of Japan’s quarterly total, so a single quarter may overstate the underlying run rate.
- Regulatory Friction: A JETRO survey cited by NITI Aayog officials found about 72% of Japanese manufacturers in India said Bureau of Indian Standards certification under Quality Control Orders had affected or would affect them, rising to more than 92% in general machinery, and about 43% of affected firms reported suspended sales or delayed deliveries.
- Tax Procedures: In a wider JETRO survey, time-consuming tax procedures were the most cited investment-related concern among Japanese firms.
- Uneven Monthly Flows: India’s total FDI slowed after April, and the sharp fall in US investment shows how quickly sources of capital can change.
- Missing Middle: Large groups such as Suzuki, Nippon Steel, and SoftBank dominate the story, while mid-size Japanese suppliers need more single-window support on land, incentives, and certification.
- Trade Balance and Market Access: India is seeking a more balanced trade relationship with Japan, and the CEPA review is still under way.
How Will Different Industries Be Affected?
- Banking, Financial Services, and NBFCs
Japanese capital from MUFG and SMBC strengthens the balance sheets and lending capacity of Indian lenders such as Shriram Finance and Yes Bank, and signals confidence in India’s credit market.
- Automobiles and Industrial Manufacturing
Suzuki, Toyota, and Daikin are expanding plants and R&D, and India is increasingly an export base, with about two-thirds of Suzuki’s India-made cars going to more than 100 countries.
- Semiconductors and Electronics
Renesas, Tokyo Electron, and Tata Electronics projects support India’s push to build chip assembly, testing, and equipment capacity, and Goyal has said Indian semiconductor demand could reach $150 billion by 2032.
- Clean Energy and Green Fuels
Japanese companies are investing in renewable energy, green methanol, green ammonia, and biogas, including a biogas plant in Assam involving Suzuki R&D and the National Dairy Development Board.
- Infrastructure and Industrial Real Estate
Japanese industrial townships and yen loans of about JPY 275.9 billion for urban transport, healthcare, and agriculture continue a long record of Japanese development finance for Indian infrastructure.
Opportunities Created by Rising Japanese Investment
Growing Japanese capital is creating opportunities in:
- Industrial townships and logistics parks: Japanese companies can invest in factories, warehouses, and transport facilities to support business operations.
- Auto and EV components: Growing investment can create demand for electric vehicle parts, batteries, and automotive components.
- Semiconductor ecosystem: Opportunities are emerging in chip assembly, testing, equipment, and supporting services.
- Banking and NBFC partnerships: Japanese financial institutions can partner with Indian lenders to expand financing for businesses and customers.
- Renewable energy: Investment in clean energy, green fuels, and biogas can support India’s energy transition.
- AI data centers: Rising demand for AI and cloud services can attract investment in data centers and computing infrastructure.
- Tier-II and Tier-III partnerships: Smaller Indian cities and local suppliers can benefit from new business partnerships, jobs, and technology transfer.
- Testing and compliance services: More investment creates demand for product testing, certification, quality checks, and regulatory support.

articles.title: Beyond Mineral Wealth: Uzbekistan’s Opportunity to Build a Strategic Industry - CFI.co | Capital Finance International
articles.summary: Beyond Mineral Wealth: Uzbekistan’s Opportunity to Build a Strategic Industry  CFI.co | Capital Finance International
articles.full_text:
A central Uzbek challenge is to turn international interest in the country’s natural resources into lasting industrial development.
By Lord Waverley | office@lordwaverley.com
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s forthcoming visit to Samarkand reflects a broader adjustment in American policy. He will attend the C5+1 ministerial with the foreign ministers of the five Central Asian states, leading a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders. Central Asia is increasingly being viewed through the lenses of economic security, access to strategic materials, transport infrastructure and regional stability, rather than primarily through its proximity to Afghanistan.
This shift creates opportunities for Uzbekistan and raises questions about the terms on which the country should engage with foreign investors. Competition over critical minerals has become an important element of international economic policy. Governments are seeking to diversify supply chains, particularly those associated with rare earth elements and other materials essential to advanced manufacturing.
Washington’s interest in Uzbekistan fits within this effort to reduce exposure to concentrated processing networks and establish alternative sources of supply. It is not alone. The UK also treats critical minerals as a government priority. This month, during a visit to Tashkent led by the Minister of State for Trade, Lord Anas Sarwar, a 2026–2028 roadmap was signed with the Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex (TMK), the state company at the centre of the sector. Its stated focus is high-technology production from tungsten, molybdenum, rhenium, lithium and rare earths.
From geological deposits to industrial capacity
In February, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Minister, Bakhtiyor Saidov, and US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau signed a memorandum of understanding on securing supply in the mining and processing of critical minerals and rare earths. Its title is instructive: securing supply comes first. Rubio’s visit could help translate that framework into commercial projects.
Yet the presence of American companies, the signing of agreements and the announcement of large investment commitments will not, by themselves, demonstrate that the partnership is succeeding. The more important question is whether cooperation will strengthen Uzbekistan’s domestic productive capacity.
Countries that export unprocessed minerals generally capture only a limited share of the economic value generated by those resources. Extracting the material is only the beginning. For rare earths, the further stages can include chemical separation, purification, metal production, alloy manufacturing and the fabrication of permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, electronics and military technologies.
Each additional stage can generate specialised employment, technical knowledge and opportunities for domestic suppliers. If Uzbekistan remains confined to supplying raw materials, much of that value will be captured abroad. If it develops competitive processing and manufacturing capabilities, the benefits could extend well beyond the mining sector.
The objective, therefore, should not simply be to attract capital into mineral extraction. It should be to determine which parts of the production process can realistically be established within Uzbekistan, and how foreign investment can help develop them.
Why local processing is difficult to establish
Developing a mineral-processing industry is considerably more complicated than opening a mine. Established producers benefit from extensive industrial networks, experienced workforces, reliable infrastructure, specialised machinery and close links between manufacturers and research institutions.
China’s position in rare earth processing illustrates the importance of these advantages. Its competitiveness reflects decades of industrial development and the concentration of complementary capabilities within an established production system. Uzbekistan would need to build many of these foundations while competing against producers that already operate at scale.
The initial costs could be substantial. New facilities require dependable electricity, transport connections, water-management systems, environmental safeguards and workers with highly specialised skills. They may also face higher production costs until sufficient demand and operational experience are established.
Price competition presents another challenge. Even if a new Uzbek facility receives public assistance, it could struggle against established international producers with lower costs and more developed supply networks. If foreign competitors reduce prices sharply, the commercial viability of the new operation could deteriorate further.
This creates a dilemma for policymakers. Without targeted support, domestic processing may never become commercially viable. With poorly targeted support, Uzbekistan could end up financing inefficient facilities that survive only through repeated government assistance.
A successful strategy must therefore combine industrial ambition with commercial discipline. Public investment should help overcome clearly identified obstacles, but projects should also be evaluated against realistic demand, production costs, environmental requirements and prospects for long-term competitiveness.
The importance of accountable economic policy
Government participation will probably be necessary if Uzbekistan wants to move beyond the export of raw materials. Private investors typically prefer locations where infrastructure, suppliers and skilled workers are already available. Left entirely to market incentives, new processing operations may continue to concentrate in established industrial centres rather than in emerging producers. Public policy can help change that calculation through infrastructure development, vocational education, research partnerships, carefully structured financing and incentives for domestic production.
Yet large investment initiatives can also create opportunities for favouritism when companies compete for mining rights, tax concessions, subsidised credit or access to public infrastructure. Agreements negotiated rapidly during high-profile diplomatic visits may be particularly difficult to scrutinise if their financial and commercial terms are not adequately disclosed.
Uzbekistan should therefore treat institutional safeguards as part of its industrial strategy rather than as an administrative afterthought. Legislative scrutiny of major agreements and meaningful public accountability belong in that strategy. These protections matter to foreign investors too. Predictable regulation and transparent competition reduce uncertainty, strengthen confidence in the investment environment and make long-term industrial projects more attractive.
Negotiating a partnership that delivers more than supply security
The American delegation’s visit should give Uzbekistan an opportunity to clarify the substance of its proposed economic partnership with Washington. A central distinction must be made between agreements designed to secure access to mineral deposits and agreements intended to develop productive capabilities inside the country. The two objectives can overlap, but they are not identical.
A supply agreement might guarantee an American buyer access to Uzbek mineral output without requiring significant investment in local processing. Such an arrangement could generate export revenue and strengthen the buyer’s supply chain, but it would not create a substantial domestic industrial base. The first phase of the agreement signed in November 2025 between TMK and American Resources Corporation follows that pattern: Uzbek tungsten concentrate is to be refined in the United States.
An ambitious partnership could combine long-term purchasing commitments with investment in processing facilities, technical training, research cooperation and the development of Uzbek suppliers. Joint ventures could provide a mechanism for sharing expertise and commercial risks, and the US–Uzbekistan joint investment holding company proposed under February’s investment framework could serve as one. Cooperation between universities and laboratories could support the development of specialised skills.
The precise balance would depend on the mineral concerned, available infrastructure, expected demand and the economics of individual projects. The strongest case for deeper local processing lies in metals Uzbekistan already produces, notably tungsten and molybdenum, which Tashkent’s $4.2 billion critical minerals programme for 2026 to 2030 already targets. Rare earth magnets, where China’s lead is widest, are a longer-term ambition. The objective should be to identify the stages where local participation is economically defensible and to establish credible pathways for expanding that participation over time.
Uzbekistan should also consider how its relationships with multiple international partners can strengthen its negotiating position. Interest from the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union and China gives Tashkent opportunities to compare investment proposals and seek better commercial and technological terms. On paper, London’s new roadmap leans towards processing inside the country; the tests set out below apply to it as fully as to any American proposal.
Nevertheless, competition between external powers does not automatically produce favourable outcomes for the host country. Its benefits depend on the quality of negotiations, the government’s ability to evaluate complex projects and the willingness of investors to make commitments that extend beyond resource procurement.

articles.title: Telangana’s Semiconductor Moment: Why Chip Design Will Define India’s Global Standing - Bisinfotech
articles.summary: Telangana’s Semiconductor Moment: Why Chip Design Will Define India’s Global Standing  Bisinfotech
articles.full_text:
For years, India’s semiconductor ambitions were measured by a single question: when will the country build its first fab?
That question is changing.
The future of semiconductors will not be decided by fabrication plants alone. It will be shaped by the countries that control chip architecture, intellectual property, system design, verification, and the engineering talent that turns ideas into silicon. On that front, Telangana is emerging as one of India’s strongest assets.
The rise of Hyderabad as a semiconductor design hub is not an accident. It is the result of years of investment in talent, research, infrastructure, and industry partnerships. As global supply chains diversify and artificial intelligence reshapes computing, Telangana has an opportunity to strengthen not only its own technology ecosystem, but also India’s position in the global chip design value chain.
The center of gravity is shifting toward design
Modern semiconductors are no longer just pieces of hardware. They are complex systems that combine computing, memory, connectivity, software, and artificial intelligence. Designing these systems requires highly specialized expertise in VLSI design, verification, physical design, firmware, and systems engineering.
India already possesses a significant advantage in this domain. The country employs nearly 20 percent of the world’s semiconductor design workforce and hosts around 7 percent of global semiconductor GCCs. Indian engineers are contributing to the design of some of the world’s most advanced chips, including technologies at the 2-nanometer node.
The next challenge is ownership.
India must move beyond being an engineering back office and become a creator of semiconductor intellectual property, system architectures, and commercially viable products. This transition will depend heavily on regional ecosystems that can combine talent, research, and entrepreneurship. Telangana is positioning itself at the center of that shift.
Why Hyderabad has become a magnet for chip design
More than 250 electronics and hardware companies operate in the state, employing over 50,000 professionals across multiple segments. Telangana has also established dedicated ESDM clusters in Raviryala and Maheshwaram to support electronics and semiconductor investments.
What makes Hyderabad different is the density of design expertise concentrated in one geography. Engineers here are working across the semiconductor value chain. This density matters because semiconductor development is inherently collaborative. A mature ecosystem allows capabilities to develop alongside one another and enables increasingly complex semiconductor programmes to be executed from India.
Design is India’s strongest entry point
The global semiconductor race is often framed as a contest for fabrication capacity. Manufacturing is important, but design offers India a faster and more sustainable path to leadership.
Building a cutting-edge fab requires billions of dollars and years of execution. Building world-class design capabilities requires talent, research institutions, access to tools, and strong industry collaboration.
The Indian government has recognized this reality. Under the Design Linked Incentive scheme, twenty-four semiconductor design projects have already been approved, while more than one hundred startups and MSMEs have received access to industry-standard EDA tools through ChipIn. Universities across the country are training tens of thousands of students in advanced chip design.
Semicon 2.0 takes this approach further. The program explicitly prioritizes chip design, semiconductor IP creation, research, and talent development alongside manufacturing expansion. The government has identified design as the foundation for positioning India as a major semiconductor IP nation.
For Telangana, this creates an important opportunity. The state has been shaping policy frameworks to attract semiconductor and electronics investments, with proposed incentives covering wafer fabrication, compound semiconductors, OSAT, ATMP and advanced R&D
The state does not need to replicate Silicon Valley or Taiwan. It needs to build on its existing strengths and create an ecosystem where startups, universities, research centers, and global firms collaborate to design the next generation of chips.
The age of AI demands a new semiconductor ecosystem
Artificial intelligence is transforming the semiconductor industry faster than any previous technological wave.
AI workloads demand faster processors, more efficient memory architectures, advanced interconnects, and specialized accelerators. Every breakthrough in artificial intelligence increases the demand for sophisticated chip design.
This shift plays directly into Hyderabad’s strengths.
The city has already established itself as a centre for software engineering, cloud computing, and data science. Combining these capabilities with semiconductor expertise creates an environment where hardware and software innovation can happen together.
Our own experience of building a semiconductor design company in Hyderabad has reinforced this belief. At Nanopowered Technologies, we work across the semiconductor design lifecycle, from architecture and RTL design through verification, physical design, analog and mixed-signal design, design-for-test and post-silicon validation. Our teams have worked across advanced technology nodes, supporting the journey from design through tape-out and silicon validation. Being able to build these capabilities from Hyderabad demonstrates what the city’s engineering ecosystem can support when specialised semiconductor expertise, talent and global technology requirements come together.
For startups and the broader ecosystem of fabless companies emerging across India, this convergence opens new possibilities. Innovation will increasingly happen at the intersection of semiconductor design, edge computing, AI acceleration, and energy efficiency.
From talent capital to innovation capital
India’s semiconductor ambition cannot end with assembling chips designed elsewhere. The real measure of success will be whether Indian companies own critical intellectual property, develop globally competitive products, and solve the technological challenges of the future.
Telangana has already built the foundations. It has the universities, the engineering talent, the industrial base, and the policy framework. The next step is to transform that foundation into a self-sustaining innovation engine.
The global semiconductor map is being redrawn. Supply chains are shifting. New technologies are emerging. Countries are competing for technological sovereignty.
In that race, Telangana’s greatest contribution may not come from the chips it manufactures. It may come from the chips it imagines first.

articles.title: The race to attract high-tech FDI: What does Vietnam need to do to pull ahead? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The race to attract high-tech FDI: What does Vietnam need to do to pull ahead?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
India is spending heavily to support mobile phone production, increasing competitive pressure.
 Investment in Vietnam continues to grow positively, with registered capital reaching US$50.36 billion in the first nine months, up 76.4%; disbursed capital is estimated at US$21.07 billion, up 12.1% compared to the same period last year, the highest in the past five years.
 According to the Foreign Investment Agency ( Ministry of Finance ), this figure continues to show that Vietnam is a preferred destination. However, in its latest report on FDI attraction, the Foreign Investment Agency once again affirmed that competition to attract high-tech projects, data centers, semiconductors, AI, and digital infrastructure in the region is becoming increasingly fierce.
 This warning has been issued not just this month, but for many months now, in reports on Vietnam's FDI attraction situation, by the Foreign Investment Agency.
 Figures cited by the Foreign Investment Agency show that Thailand recorded a 37% year-on-year increase in investment applications in the first half of 2026, reaching US$43.6 billion, with registered FDI capital surging 80% to US$40.5 billion, largely driven by a wave of investment in digital infrastructure and AI data centers. Malaysia also continues to strengthen its position as a regional data and AI hub in Johor with a series of large investment commitments from global technology corporations. 
|  | 
| India has spent a large amount of money to support mobile phone manufacturers. | 
 In reality, to compete in attracting FDI, countries have announced many important policies. For example, Thailand earlier this year announced a key strategy to accelerate its transformation from a traditional processing center to a "semiconductor powerhouse" in Southeast Asia. To realize this ambition, Thailand has not only offered tariff incentives but has also developed a comprehensive support package, including direct funding for research and development (R&D), implementing a special visa policy to attract international talent, and committing to providing "ultra-stable" infrastructure with a clean power grid and specialized water management system for silicon wafer manufacturing plants…
 Malaysia has also announced a national action plan for 2026-2030 aimed at dramatically transforming its position from a technology consumer to a domestic innovative manufacturer. Two years ago, the government also decided to allocate up to US$5.3 billion to the National Semiconductor Strategy, with the goal of attracting US$110 billion in domestic and foreign investment for the development of the semiconductor industry, while also training 60,000 personnel for this sector…
 And notably, India announced its Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) 2026 at the end of August 2026. The MPMS is designed to link the growth of production and revenue for businesses with the use of domestically sourced components as well as design, research, and development (R&D) activities.
 A notable aspect of MPMS is that support is determined based on the actual performance of the business. For large-scale manufacturers, the support amount is calculated based on the portion of revenue exceeding the standard revenue threshold. Businesses that reach a certain revenue threshold and continue to maintain growth will be eligible for support.
 This mechanism also encourages businesses to increase their use of components sourced from the Indian market. Phones using domestically sourced components can receive an additional subsidy of up to 1.5%. These components include screens, cameras, phone casings, batteries, and charging cables.
 Indian domestic brands are eligible for higher levels of support if they meet conditions regarding ownership structure, operational control, and intellectual property rights, while also establishing design and research centers within the country. Thus, the level of support depends not only on size and revenue growth but also on the extent of participation in the domestic supply chain, as well as design and R&D activities.
 To implement the MPMS, India has allocated 62,500 crore rupees, equivalent to approximately US$7.5 billion. The program spans five fiscal years, from 2026-2027 to 2030-2031, with grants determined based on business performance.
 The design of the MPMS shows that India is not simply allocating resources to increase mobile phone production. By linking support levels to business results and specific business activities, the program simultaneously aims at three goals: expanding revenue, increasing the use of domestically sourced components, and bringing more design and R&D activities into India.
 In fact, this is not the first time India has announced this policy. A few years ago, India also implemented the Production Linked Incentive Scheme (PLI), which just ended on March 31st. Under that scheme, India also allocated a large sum of money to subsidize each phone produced.
 Thanks to this "boost," information indicates that during the four years of implementing the PLI (Private Partnership in India), from 2022 to 2025, India's smartphone exports increased more than sevenfold, from $3.1 billion to $24.1 billion. By 2025, smartphones will become the country's largest export item.
 This result lays the groundwork for India to move to the next phase in its mobile phone industry development strategy. Instead of focusing solely on expanding manufacturing and assembly, India aims to become a global mobile phone manufacturing and export hub, while also integrating its domestic supply chain more deeply into the process.
 What does Vietnam need to do to move forward?
 Although Vietnam still holds a significant advantage in the race to attract FDI, the pressure is increasing. At the recent "Go Global Bac Ninh 2026" forum, Vice Chairman of the Bac Ninh Provincial People's Committee Pham Van Thinh frankly mentioned the need to "compete" with manufacturing hubs in the region and the world , such as Thailand and Malaysia.
 According to Mr. Pham Van Thinh, Bac Ninh, as well as Vietnam, "doesn't have much time left" to build its position as a key global supply hub. "This opportunity may only last for about 5 years," Mr. Thinh said, adding that by 2031-2032, the number of large-scale factories relocating to this market will be significantly reduced.
 The challenge is what Vietnam needs to do to both retain existing investors and attract more high-quality FDI in fields such as electronics, semiconductors, and AI, in order to realize the goals set out in Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW of the Politburo on the Development of the Foreign-Invested Economy. 
|  | 
| Vietnam is continuing to improve its institutions and policies to attract investment in high-tech sectors. | 
 Speaking at a recent event on this matter, Deputy Minister of Finance Tran Quoc Phuong stated that the Government recently issued Resolution No. 280/NQ-CP on the Action Plan to implement Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW. Accordingly, the Ministry of Finance is tasked with institutionalizing the mechanisms and policies outlined in Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW, including further improving the institutional framework, enhancing the investment and business environment, developing flexible incentive mechanisms for core projects, and promoting linkages between the domestic economy and the FDI sector…
 “Vietnam is currently making policy adjustments towards greater competitiveness. The 2025 Investment Law has simplified approval procedures and opened a ‘green channel’ to accelerate strategic technology projects such as semiconductors, AI, and data. These are necessary efforts for Vietnam to maintain its position as a preferred destination, alongside the need for continued rapid improvement in electricity infrastructure, logistics, and high-quality human resources,” Deputy Minister Tran Quoc Phuong said.
 Meanwhile, Ms. Bui Thu Thuy, Deputy Director of the Foreign Investment Department, said that the Investment Law is also being proposed for amendment and supplementation. The draft law will focus on major directions, including reshaping the investment attraction map by region and establishing specific, superior incentive mechanisms, including "negotiating" incentives with major investment partners.
 To increase its attractiveness, Vietnam has also utilized its Investment Support Fund, which includes providing cash support for activities such as R&D, fixed asset investment, and high-tech product manufacturing.
 However, the Investment Support Fund is designed for multiple sectors, rather than focusing on a specific industry, as India is doing. With MPMS, India selects a specific industry, clearly defining the desired outcomes, from revenue growth and domestic supply chain development to bringing design and R&D activities domestically, and then links the level of support to each of those outcomes.
 In the context of limited support resources and increasingly fierce competition for investment, the selection of priority sectors and the level of resource concentration have become crucial factors in policy design and implementation. Focusing more on a few industries and sectors with the potential to create high added value, form supply chains, and disseminate technology can help support resources have a more significant impact, rather than allocating them too broadly.
 From this perspective, India's MPMS policy could serve as a valuable reference as Vietnam gradually shifts from traditional incentives to performance-based support mechanisms in the future.
