articles.title: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize - The Dispatch
articles.summary: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize  The DispatchPillay decries US sanctions on ICC, where she is ‘confident’ Netanyahu will one day stand trial  The Times of IsraelTrump swipes at Nobel committee after peace prize awarded to human rights lawyer  PoliticoMy relative defined ‘genocide.’ Honoring him means scrutinizing Navi Pillay’s Israel findings.  Jewish Telegraphic AgencyAnalysing Africa newsletter: A Nobel and ignoble day for the rule of l...
articles.full_text:
It’s not every day that an Islamist death cult celebrates the announcement of the Nobel Peace Prize winner, but that is exactly what happened on Friday evening when Hamas welcomed the selection of Navi Pillay as “an important step toward international justice.” Why is Oslo’s humanitarian hero winning applause from an Iranian-backed terror proxy that massacred families and kidnapped children?
I have dealt with Pillay in Geneva since she arrived here in 2008 as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights. Over 18 years, I watched her turn the language of universal rights into a weapon aimed relentlessly at the Jewish state.
It began with a welcome. In September 2008, my team at U.N. Watch publicly saluted her struggle against South African apartheid. Her story deserved respect. But already then, her first act as U.N. human rights chief was to champion Durban II, the planned Geneva follow-up to the notorious 2001 conference in South Africa, where an ostensible campaign against racism became a festival of antisemitism.
At Durban I, thousands of radical activists marched against Israel and Jews, some carrying signs praising Adolf Hitler. Jewish students were threatened. The Arab Lawyers Union handed out cartoons of hook-nosed Jews. Copies of The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the notorious antisemitic forgery, were openly distributed. At the NGO Forum, Israel was declared a “racist apartheid state” and accused of “genocide.” In the Durban outcome document, the Jewish state alone was singled out as a perpetrator of racism. Rep. Tom Lantos, a Holocaust survivor, called it “the most sickening and unabashed display of hate for Jews” he had witnessed since the Nazi era.
Pillay wanted to rehabilitate Durban. We wanted to prevent a repeat. Alarm bells started ringing when Muammar Gaddafi’s Libyan regime was appointed chair of the preparatory committee, and Iran the vice chair.
Months before the April 2009 conference, Pillay was already rebuking the U.S., Canada, and Israel for threatening to boycott, dismissing their “all or nothing” approach, and warning against “pretexts for inaction.” In the end, Canada, Italy, the U.S., Germany, Australia, and the Netherlands were among 10 countries that boycotted.
When Durban II finally opened, Holocaust denier Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, then president of Iran, was the first head of state to speak. He used the Geneva podium to denounce Israel’s existence. France, along with many other European delegations, walked out of the room in protest. Pillay defended Ahmadinejad’s right to speak, and urged against more countries pulling out of the conference.
That same year, after Hamas and Israel fought a three-week war, the U.N. Human Rights Council condemned Israel and created a commission of inquiry. Pillay recruited Richard Goldstone to serve as chair, with her staff doing most of the work. The inquiry’s September 2009 report was a bombshell, accusing Israel’s political and military leaders of a “deliberately disproportionate attack designed to punish, humiliate and terrorize a civilian population.” It called for action by the International Criminal Court, and for criminal proceedings in foreign courts under universal jurisdiction.
The report was a travesty of justice. A year and a half later, in a Washington Post op-ed, Goldstone himself retracted the core charge.
It later emerged that Pillay’s office had hired Grietje Baars, a radical Marxist law professor, to write key sections of the report. Before joining the investigation, Baars had already described Israel’s operation as a “massacre.” While working on it, Baars signed a declaration denouncing Israel’s “apartheid regime.” The next year, in 2010, Baars joined the Hamas-backed Gaza flotilla campaign as a European spokesman.
Under Pillay’s leadership, this is what passed for fact-finding at the U.N. I later submitted a legal complaint to the secretary-general about Pillay’s hiring of Baars. I received no reply.
Pillay herself “strongly condemned” Israel’s use of force as “disproportionate” as soon as the fighting began. Her verdict preceded the examination. By contrast, joining the U.S. and Canada, German Chancellor Angela Merkel stated that Israel had a right to self-defense and that responsibility for the conflict lay “clearly and exclusively” with Hamas. Even U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs John Holmes spoke out against “the reckless and cynical use of civilian installations by Hamas.” Not Pillay.
In January 2009, after years of rocket attacks from Gaza, Israel imposed a naval blockade to prevent weapons reaching Hamas by sea. In May 2010, Turkey’s terrorist-linked IHH organized a flotilla which set out to breach it. When Israeli commandos boarded its lead ship, the Mavi Marmara, they were attacked by militants wielding iron bars, clubs, chains, and slingshots.
Within hours, Pillay declared that Israel treated international law with “perpetual disdain,” denouncing the blockade as “inhumane and illegal.” Yet the subsequent Palmer inquiry appointed by the U.N. secretary-general concluded that the naval blockade was lawful—a legitimate security measure to prevent weapons from entering Gaza by sea. Again, Pillay’s verdict came before she examined the facts—or the law.
By 2014, Pillay had endorsed the charge that when Palestinian men beat their wives, it’s Israel’s fault. “Women with husbands explained that the dire economic situation and the pressures of the occupation have made men more violent because they have lost their ability to provide and protect — two essential elements of manhood in a traditional patriarchal society,” Special Rapporteur Yakin Ertürk wrote in 2005, following her visit to Palestinian territories. “As men become stripped of their manhood, women become the shock absorbers of the crises as targets of domestic violence.” Nine years later, Pillay reported to the U.N. that this analysis “remains valid.”
After leaving the U.N. human rights office in 2014, Pillay dropped any pretense of distance. In 2020, she signed a campaign titled “Sanction Apartheid Israel!” In June 2021, she joined a letter blaming Israeli “domination and oppression” for the previous month’s war, which began with Hamas firing rockets at Jerusalem and other Israeli cities.
A month later, the president of the Human Rights Council—Nazhat Shameem Khan, now a deputy prosecutor of the International Criminal Court—appointed Pillay to chair an inquiry into the very conflict for which she had already blamed Israel. But its mandate went even further: a permanent investigation of alleged violations before and after the 2021 clash, reaching into the conflict’s “underlying root causes,” with no end date. The campaigner became the investigator, and Pillay’s verdict came with her appointment.
In February 2022, U.N. Watch submitted a detailed legal brief requesting Pillay’s recusal. We cited her statements and the U.N.’s own impartiality standards. We received no reply.
That June, I walked up to Pillay at the Human Rights Council and handed her a copy. She acknowledged having seen our motion.
“We never received a reply,” I said.
“We can’t respond to everything,” she answered.
Everything? This was a core challenge to her fitness to preside. A few days ago, Pillay claimed that her inquiry “essentially worked like a court.” Yet a judge cannot dismiss a recusal motion as unwanted correspondence.
Later, in July 2022, her fellow commissioner Miloon Kothari railed against “the Jewish lobby” and questioned Israel’s U.N. membership. Pillay defended him, claiming his remarks had been taken out of context. In the end, Kothari retracted his comments after numerous democracies condemned him for antisemitism, as did the Human Rights Council chair himself. Pillay never recanted.
In September 2025, the Pillay inquiry fulfilled its purpose: It accused Israel of genocide. The report was built on selective quotations used to infer genocidal intent, and a complete sidelining of Hamas’ military infrastructure and use of civilian sites. According to the Pillay report’s chronology, it was Israel that attacked on October 7.
Pillay’s accusation of genocide against Israel appears to be what prompted the Nobel. Her earlier achievements—as a judge in South Africa and on the U.N.’s Rwanda tribunal—were known for decades. That record deserves recognition. But it also makes her disregard for impartiality harder to excuse.
She knew the standards. A reputation earned in one courtroom cannot exempt its owner from scrutiny in another. Nor can past courage transform a partisan investigation into justice simply because its findings carry the United Nations seal.
Pillay was named to the inquiry for her authority as a judge, but she acted on the commitments of a campaigner. The Nobel Committee is now seeking to magnify her imprimatur.
Hamas understands the benefit perfectly. Its war against Israel gains a prestigious legal vocabulary, and its victims recede behind an indictment of the state that defended them. That is why Hamas cheered. The Nobel Committee should now tell the world whether this is its desired outcome.

articles.title: Rising Tech Demand and Infrastructure Investments Drive Higher 2026 Thailand Trade Flows - LM - Logistics Manager
articles.summary: Rising Tech Demand and Infrastructure Investments Drive Higher 2026 Thailand Trade Flows  LM - Logistics Manager
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s expanding electronics trade and investment in digital infrastructure are creating opportunities for logistics providers, while a widening merchandise trade deficit and uncertainty over international trade conditions demand careful planning.
Thailand’s trade expansion in 2026 is bringing a changing mix of cargo through the country’s international supply chains. Electronics, computing equipment and machinery feature prominently in both imports and exports, reflecting Thailand’s participation in technology manufacturing and the growing importance of investment in digital infrastructure. For logistics providers, the opportunity extends beyond moving more goods to meeting the different handling, delivery and supply chain requirements of these industries.
During the first eight months of 2026, Thailand’s exports reached USD 266.150 billion, increasing by 18.9% year over year, while imports rose by 36.1% to USD 303.987 billion. The resulting merchandise trade deficit of USD 37.837 billion highlights the faster expansion of imports, even as exports continued to grow strongly.
These figures provide an important measure of trading activity, but their implications for logistics require closer examination. Higher trade values do not translate directly into equivalent increases in container volumes or freight demand. Cargo composition, shipment size and transport requirements determine where opportunities emerge. Understanding that distinction will be essential for businesses seeking to respond to Thailand’s changing trade profile.
Electronics Lead the Export Mix
Technology products occupy a leading position in Thailand’s export structure. Automatic data processing machines and their parts were the largest export category during January–August, generating USD 37.510 billion and accounting for 14.09% of total exports. Telephone sets contributed a further USD 11.729 billion, while electronic integrated circuits accounted for USD 8.732 billion.
Together, these categories underline the importance of electronics to Thailand’s international trade. Demand associated with artificial intelligence and investment in technology infrastructure is supporting the sector, although the broad product classifications encompass applications beyond AI alone.
For logistics operators, electronics present requirements that differ from those of many traditional industrial goods. Depending on the product, shipments may require secure handling, suitable packaging and close control over delivery schedules. Manufacturers also need reliable inbound supplies of components to support production and predictable outbound services to meet customer commitments.
The commercial opportunity therefore lies in providing dependable services throughout the manufacturing cycle. Customs clearance, shipment visibility and coordination between international transport and domestic delivery can help customers manage production schedules and respond when orders or delivery requirements change.
Thailand’s export base nevertheless remains diverse. Motor cars, parts and accessories were the second-largest category, with exports worth USD 20.736 billion, representing 7.79% of the total. Machinery and parts contributed USD 8.858 billion, followed by plastic pellets, chemical products, air conditioning machines and parts, and pneumatic tires and inner tubes.
This diversity supports demand across different logistics services. Technology cargo may attract greater attention, but automotive and other industrial supply chains continue to provide substantial business for freight forwarders, transport operators and warehouse providers.
Imports Reflect a Changing Investment Profile
The import figures offer another perspective on Thailand’s evolving industrial activity. Electronic integrated circuits were the largest import category during the first eight months, reaching USD 43.133 billion and accounting for 14.19% of total imports. Electrical machinery and parts followed at USD 33.959 billion, or 11.17%.
Machinery and parts added USD 18.008 billion, while automatic data processing machines and parts accounted for USD 13.784 billion. These categories are consistent with demand for manufacturing inputs, equipment and technology infrastructure, although the statistics do not identify how much of each category was destined specifically for AI or data center projects.
For logistics businesses, investment-related imports can create opportunities at several stages. Equipment must move from its overseas supplier through customs and onward to a factory, warehouse or installation site. Where shipments involve large or sensitive machinery, customers may also require specialized handling, delivery planning and coordination with site teams.
Data center development illustrates the potential complexity. Equipment deliveries may need to follow construction and installation schedules, with storage or staged release where sites are not ready to receive every shipment at once. The service requirement can therefore extend beyond international freight to include domestic transport and management of delivery timing.
However, technology is only part of the import picture. Crude oil represented USD 27.600 billion, or 9.08% of imports, while gold accounted for USD 20.921 billion. Chemical products, metal ores and products, vehicles and transport equipment, and iron and steel also featured among the leading categories.
These differences matter when assessing the widening trade deficit. The balance reflects the value of a broad range of imported goods and cannot be attributed solely to digital infrastructure investment. Nor does it provide a complete measure of the performance of individual logistics segments.
Major Trading Partners Shape Service Demand
Thailand’s leading trading partners reveal where international logistics connections remain particularly important. China supplied USD 94.322 billion of imports during January–August, accounting for 31.03% of the total. Taiwan followed with USD 32.742 billion, or 10.77%, while Japan contributed USD 21.023 billion, representing 6.92%.
Electrical machinery and parts were identified as key imports from China, electronic integrated circuits from Taiwan, and machinery and parts from Japan. These trading relationships reinforce the importance of reliable connections between Thailand and Asian manufacturing centers.
For manufacturers, the availability of imported inputs can influence production schedules and their ability to fulfill export orders. Logistics providers serving these customers need to understand both sides of the supply chain, including how an inbound delay could affect subsequent outbound shipments.
The United States was Thailand’s largest export market, receiving USD 64.733 billion of goods and accounting for 24.32% of exports. Automatic data processing machines and parts were identified as a key product category in this trade.
China ranked second among export destinations, with USD 30.531 billion, followed by Japan at USD 17.937 billion. Singapore and Australia completed the top five, receiving USD 12.114 billion and USD 11.482 billion respectively.
The range of markets also brings varied cargo requirements. Thailand’s exports to China include fresh, frozen and dried fruits, while motor cars, parts and accessories are important shipments to Japan and Australia. Maintaining services suited to these established trades remains important alongside developing capabilities for technology customers.
Growth Brings Greater Planning Demands
Thailand began 2026 with strong trade momentum. First-quarter exports increased by 17.6% year over year to approximately USD 96.170 billion, while imports rose by 32.4% to USD 105.646 billion. By the end of June, cumulative exports had reached USD 196.741 billion and imports USD 228.485 billion.
The continued expansion through August points to substantial activity across international supply chains. However, businesses must distinguish sustained customer demand from shipments brought forward in response to uncertainty over tariffs or other trade measures.
Accelerating shipments can protect customers against an anticipated change, but it can also shift demand between periods. For logistics providers, this complicates decisions about transport capacity, warehouse space and staffing. Close communication with customers is needed to establish whether a booking increase reflects a lasting requirement or a temporary adjustment.
Planning must also account for geopolitical developments and their potential effects on energy prices, freight rates and transport costs. Disruption affecting an international route can influence delivery schedules and the commercial viability of individual shipments.
The practical response is to maintain clear communication over available services, expected transit times and alternative arrangements. Customers benefit when logistics partners identify potential difficulties early enough to support decisions on purchasing, production and delivery.
Building Capability Around the Cargo
Thailand’s changing trade profile presents opportunities for providers able to match their services to specific customer requirements. Electronics manufacturers may place particular emphasis on secure handling and dependable delivery schedules. Machinery importers may need support with installation-related deliveries, while agricultural exporters require services appropriate to product condition and shelf life.
These requirements call for targeted capability development. Trade growth alone does not establish the case for expanding every service or investing in every type of facility. Providers need to examine the cargo they handle, the customers they serve and the consistency of demand before committing resources.
The outlook for the remaining months of 2026 will depend partly on the durability of technology demand and developments in international trade policy. Electronics and infrastructure investment remain importan

articles.summary: China's Lithium Market New Player: World's Most Profitable Oil Company Enters Lithium Carbonate Industry - A Game-Changing Partnership for China's Lithium Dream  36Kr
articles.full_text:
China's "Lithium" Dream Partner? The world's most profitable oil company also joins the fray in the lithium carbonate market.
China Energy Net & China Energy Storage learned that multiple foreign media outlets reported recently that Saudi Aramco has signed a lithium demonstration project agreement with US oilfield service firm NESR, to invest in and build a battery-grade lithium carbonate demonstration project in the Saudi desert region.
The project is designed with an annual output of 2,000 tons of battery-grade lithium carbonate, which is scheduled to be completed and put into operation at the end of 2027. The whole project is constructed on a turnkey basis, with a total contract value of up to about 200 million US dollars.
Saudi Aramco is a global leading oil enterprise. In the first half of 2026, the company's net profit reached as high as 67.2 billion US dollars, a year-on-year increase of 29.2%; its full-year net profit in 2025 was 92.8 billion US dollars. Although it declined compared with previous years, it remains the most profitable oil company in the world.
The entry of the world's most profitable oil company into the lithium carbonate market has naturally drawn extremely high attention from the whole industry.
In addition, against the current backdrop of global energy transition, lithium carbonate has become the focus of competition among all countries. As this oil giant acts as a "catfish" to disrupt the market, what changes will take place in the lithium carbonate market? Will it be a boon or a bane for China?
Innovative Lithium Carbonate Extraction Method
Different from current lithium carbonate players in various countries, Saudi Aramco has taken a unique technical path in this foray into the lithium carbonate sector.
According to NESR, the core technology adopted in this project is NESR's LiThara™ platform, which relies neither on traditional mining nor solar evaporation, but uses direct lithium extraction technology, with raw materials taken from oilfield associated brine.
The whole process is divided into three major links: brine pretreatment, direct lithium extraction, and carbonization to synthesize lithium carbonate, which can selectively separate lithium elements directly from brine and finally produce finished battery-grade lithium carbonate products.
This can be regarded as a new idea for lithium extraction. Prior to this, the mainstream route of brine lithium extraction was still traditional salt lake lithium extraction. For example, salt lakes in South America generally adopt the solar pond evaporation process, which introduces brine into large-scale salt pans, evaporates water through solar exposure, precipitates impurities and then purifies lithium carbonate.
The traditional salt lake solar evaporation process features mature technology and low production cost; however, this method is extremely dependent on climate, requiring sufficient sunshine, occupying large areas of land, and having a long production cycle. The complete production process takes several months, and it is greatly disturbed by seasonal fluctuations such as rainfall, so it is only suitable for development in plateau salt lake resource areas.
In contrast, the DLE direct lithium extraction technology does not require large-scale evaporation and salt drying, greatly reduces the land occupation, and even shortens the production cycle to a few days, with fewer constraints on site conditions. Regions without plateau salt lake resources such as Saudi Arabia can also use brine produced by oilfields to carry out lithium resource recovery.
China Energy Net & China Energy Storage noted that as early as 2024, Saudi Aramco and the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company had already explored DLE technology. Meanwhile, another oil giant ExxonMobil is also actively deploying DLE-related technologies. At that time, the industry generally believed that DLE was in the early stage and commercialization was difficult to achieve. Now two years have passed, this technology may have made new breakthroughs, which is why Saudi Aramco dares to invest 200 million US dollars to expand this business.
It is worth mentioning that, among all current lithium carbonate extraction technology routes, brine lithium extraction has the lowest cost. For example, the gross profit margin of lithium carbonate products of Zangge Mining, a domestic salt lake lithium extraction giant, once exceeded 95%, comparable to that of Moutai. This is also an important reason why Saudi Aramco dares to place such a large bet on this business.
Will It Be Beneficial to China?
For Saudi Aramco, deploying lithium carbonate business is not a simple cross-sector move.
A large amount of associated brine will be continuously produced during the exploitation of major oilfields in the Middle East. In the past, these associated brines were classified as oilfield production waste that required special treatment. The DLE technology essentially converts the waste liquid that would have been treated into key raw materials for lithium batteries. Saudi Aramco's "waste recycling" in this move can be described as killing two birds with one stone, and can even improve the company's performance.
China Energy Net & China Energy Storage noted that nowadays, under the background of global energy transition, lithium is known as the "white oil" of the electric era and has been classified as a key strategic mineral by many countries.
As early as 2017, the United States began to build an exclusive "small circle" around the key mineral supply chain. In June 2022, the United States also took the lead in forming the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP), whose member states include Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, etc., focusing on the whole industrial chain collaboration of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other varieties. In August this year, Chile, Argentina, Bolivia and Peru in South America signed a joint statement to strengthen regional cooperation in the field of strategic minerals among the four countries, focusing on minerals such as copper and lithium. Not long ago, Zimbabwe in Africa also announced that it will ban the export of lithium concentrate from January 1, 2027, requiring enterprises to build lithium sulfate processing plants within its territory.
China is a major country with lithium resources and also a major lithium consumer. Data shows that from January to August this year, China's cumulative import volume of lithium carbonate reached 236,400 tons, a year-on-year increase of 54.08%. This data shows that China's lithium carbonate supply is becoming more and more dependent on foreign countries. If this data continues to rise, China may be "strangled" by the overseas market.
China Energy Net & China Energy Storage noted that the lithium carbonate project invested and built by Saudi Aramco this time has an annual output of only 2,000 tons, which can hardly make any waves in the global market, and it is difficult to change the overall global lithium supply and demand situation in the short term. However, once the DLE process is locally verified to be feasible and its cost is proven, a large amount of oilfield brine in the Middle East may become a new source of lithium.
For the global lithium battery industry chain, the supply sources of lithium resources will be more diversified in the future, and new changes will take place in the supply chain, which may be a good thing for China. It is worth mentioning that China is an in-depth participant in the energy transition process in the Middle East, and Chinese enterprises are involved in landmark projects such as the Red Sea Project. Saudi Aramco also has extensive business interactions with Chinese enterprises, and their cooperation has long gone beyond oil trading, penetrating into equity investment and many other fields. Based on this, Saudi Aramco may become an ideal lithium partner for China.
It can be said that this demonstration project of Saudi Aramco, no matter for itself, for China or for the global lithium carbonate market, has far greater strategic value than the contribution value of its actual production capacity.
This article is from the WeChat Official Account "China Energy Storage", author: Xiao Meng, authorized for release by 36Kr.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is transferring 15 metric tons (mt) of Atlantic bluefin tuna (BFT) quota from the Reserve category to the Angling category large school/small medium subquota. This transfer results in an adjusted Angling category large school/small medium subquota of 188.4 mt and an adjusted Reserve category quota of 27 mt. This action is intended to provide further harvest opportunities for Angling category fishermen, based on consideration of the regulatory determination criteria regarding inseason adjustments and applies to HMS Angling and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels when fishing recreationally for BFT.
DATES:
The quota transfer is effective October 13, 2026 through December 31, 2026.
Atlantic BFT fisheries are managed under the 2006 Consolidated HMS Fishery Management Plan (FMP) and its amendments, pursuant to the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act; 16 U.S.C. 1801et seq.) and consistent with the Atlantic Tunas Convention Act (ATCA; 16 U.S.C. 971et seq.). ATCA is the implementing statute for binding recommendations of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). The HMS FMP and its amendments are implemented by regulations at 50 CFR part 635. Section 635.27(a) divides the U.S. BFT quota, established by ICCAT and as implemented by the United States among the various domestic fishing categories, per the allocations established in the HMS FMP and its amendments. NMFS is required under the Magnuson-Stevens Act at 16 U.S.C. 1854(g)(1)(D) to provide U.S. fishing vessels with a reasonable opportunity to harvest quotas under relevant international fishery agreements such as the ICCAT Convention, which is implemented domestically pursuant to ATCA.
Every year, the BFT fishing year starts on January 1 and ends on December 31. The Angling category opens on January 1 and continues through December 31 or until the applicable quota or subquota is reached or projected to be reached, whichever comes first. NMFS recently published a final rule to implement the 2025 ICCAT recommendation 25-05 (91 FR 53526, August 19, 2026). As described in § 635.27(a), the current baseline U.S. BFT quota is 1,509.98 mt (not including the 62.5 mt ICCAT allocated to the United States to account for bycatch of BFT in pelagic longline fisheries in the vicinity of the management area boundary and adjacent areas per § 635.27(a)(3)). The baseline quotas for the Angling and Reserve categories are 341.3 mt (§ 635.27(a)(2)) and 43.8 mt (§ 635.27(a)(6)), respectively. The Angling category quota is further subdivided into subquotas by size class. Specific to this action, the subquotas are 157.2 mt for school BFT and 173.4 mt for large school/small medium BFT (
see
§ 635.27(a)(2) and (a)(2)(ii)). To date, NMFS has published several actions that have adjusted the Reserve category quota (91 FR 5855, February 10, 2026; 91 FR 43571, July 16, 2026; 91 FR 53526, August 19, 2026; 91 FR 64302, October 8, 2026). The current adjusted Reserve category quota is 42 mt.
Transfer From the Reserve Category to the Angling Category Large School/Small Medium Subquota
Under § 635.27(a)(8), NMFS has the authority to transfer quota among fishing categories or subcategories after considering the determination criteria provided under § 635.27(a)(7). This section focuses on the calculations involved in transferring quota currently available from the 2026 Reserve category to the 2026 Angling category quota; the consideration of the determination criteria can be found below after this section.
As stated above, the baseline Angling category large school/small medium subquota is 173.4 mt. The adjusted Reserve category quota is 42 mt. Transferring 15 mt from the Reserve category to the Angling category large school/small medium subquota results in an adjusted Angling category large school/small medium subquota of 188.4 mt (173.4 mt + 15 mt = 188.4 mt), and an adjusted Reserve category quota of 27 mt (42 mt−15 mt = 27 mt). With this transfer the overall Angling category quota increases to 356.3 mt (341.3 mt + 15 mt = 356.3 mt). The Angling category quota is available for use by HMS Angling and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels when fishing recreationally for BFT.
In summary, this transfer results in an adjusted Angling category large school/small medium subquota of 188.4 mt and an adjusted Reserve quota of 27 mt. The Angling category large school/small medium fishery will remain open until December 31, 2026, or until the adjusted Angling category large school/small medium subquota is reached, whichever comes first.
Consideration of the Relevant Determination Criteria
NMFS has considered all of the relevant determination criteria and their applicability to these inseason actions (§ 635.27(a)(7)). These criteria include, but are not limited to, the following:
Regarding the usefulness of information obtained from catches in the particular category for biological sampling and monitoring of the status of the stock (§ 635.27(a)(7)(i)), biological samples collected from BFT landed by recreational fishermen continue to provide NMFS with valuable parts and data for ongoing scientific studies of BFT age and growth, migration, and reproductive status. Additional opportunity to land BFT in the Angling category would support the continued collection of a broad range of data for these studies and for stock monitoring purposes.
NMFS also considered the catches of the Angling category quota to date and the likelihood of closure of that segment of the fishery if no adjustment is made (§ 635.27(a)(7)(ii). In doing so, NMFS also reviewed the latest information regarding landings and the availability of BFT on the fishing grounds (§ 635.27(a)(7)(ix)). Fishery performance in recent years indicates that in the late summer/fall the recreational fishery shifts to large school/small medium-sized BFT as these sized fish are more geographically spread out along the east coast. A quota transfer at this time should provide additional opportunities to harvest the large school/small medium subquota while avoiding exceeding the overall Angling category quota. Should recreational landings be higher or lower than expected, NMFS could take another action later in the year to further adjust the daily retention limit or close the Angling category fishery.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
On October 2, 2026, the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT) issued its final judgment in
Ellwood City Forge Company
v.
United State
s, Court no. 23-00191, sustaining the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce)'s first remand results pertaining to the administrative review of the antidumping duty (AD) order on forged steel fluid end blocks (FEBs) from Italy covering the period of review (POR) July 23, 2020 through December 31, 2021. Commerce is notifying the public that the CIT's final judgment is not in harmony with Commerce's final results of the administrative review, and that Commerce is amending the final results with respect to the dumping margin assigned to Lucchini Mame Forge S.p.A.
DATES:
Applicable October 12, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Yang Jin Chun, AD/CVD Operations, Office I, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-5760.
( printed page 65528)
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 14, 2023, Commerce published its
Final Results
of the administrative review of the antidumping duty order on forged steel fluid end blocks from Italy covering the POR July 23, 2020 through December 31, 2021. Commerce calculated a weighted-average dumping margin of 2.97 percent.[1]
Elwood City Forge Company appealed Commerce's
Final Results.
On April 28, 2026, the CIT remanded the
Final Results
to Commerce, directing Commerce to: (1) further explain its determination that Cogne and Ciscato, two producers whose financial statements Commerce used to calculate Lucchini's CV profit, produced merchandise identical to the subject FEBs; and (2) further explain/reconsider its selection of the market-price benchmark used in the major input analysis.[2]
In its final results of redetermination, issued in July 2026, Commerce reversed both determinations. Commerce excluded Cogne and Ciscato from its CV profit calculation. Commerce also used Company A's U.S. purchases of ingots as the market-price benchmark for its major-input analysis and rejected Lucchini's February 2023 adjustment information as untimely new factual information.[3]
The CIT sustained Commerce's
Final Results of Redetermination.[4]
Timken Notice
In its decision in
Timken,[5]
as clarified by
Diamond Sawblades,[6]
the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit held that, pursuant to section 516A(c) and (e) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), Commerce must publish a notice of court decision that is not “in harmony” with a Commerce determination and must suspend liquidation of entries pending a “conclusive” court decision. The CIT's October 2, 2026, judgment constitutes a final decision of the CIT that is not in harmony with Commerce's
Final Results.
Thus, this notice is published in fulfillment of the publication requirements of
Timken.
Amended Final Results
Because there is now a final court judgment, Commerce is amending its
Final Results
with respect to Lucchini as follows:

At this time, Commerce remains enjoined by CIT order from liquidating entries that: were produced and/or exported by Lucchini, and were entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption during the period of review July 23, 2020, through December 31, 2021. articles.full_text: EPA is issuing significant new use rules (SNURs) under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) for certain chemical substances that were the subject of premanufacture notices (PMNs) and are also subject to an Order issued by EPA pursuant to TSCA. The SNURs require persons to notify EPA at least 90 days before commencing the manufacture (defined by statute to include import) or processing of any of these chemical substances for an activity that is designated as a significant new use in the SNUR. The required notification initiates EPA's evaluation of the conditions of that use for that chemical substance. In addition, the manufacture or processing for the significant new use may not commence until EPA has conducted a review of the required notification; made an appropriate determination regarding that notification; and taken such actions as required by that determination.

articles.summary:

The post My excellent Conversation with Liaquat Ahamed appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is part of the episode summary:
They start with that puzzle before moving through Gladstone’s startlingly self-interested bet on Egyptian bonds, Bismarck’s role in destroying bimetallism and deflating the world economy for two decades, whether a global silver or symmetallic standard could have worked, Britain’s fateful decision to re-peg the pound to gold in 1926, Hjalmar Schacht’s transformation from the economist who stabilized Weimar’s currency to opportunist collaborator with the Nazi regime, Montagu Norman’s spiritualist beliefs, why the 1920s produced such a creative cultural moment, lessons from the IMF on Ireland’s housing bubble and Pakistan’s two dozen bailouts, what went wrong in the eurozone crisis, Britain’s baffling modern stagnation, and finally to his own restless career — from the World Bank to a failed Iraq film to Ismaili Islam’s uniquely progress-oriented leadership structure, and what he wants to write next.
We open thus:
COWEN: I have a general question about how your work fits together. Your book Lords of Finance, it convinced me that financial crises really matter, and your new book, 1873, almost convinced me that financial crises don’t really matter, because the world just keeps on growing. What makes the difference for when, historically speaking, crises will really matter?
AHAMED: I think the first book, Lords of Finance, was about the financial crisis that really plunged the world into a Great Depression. The second, 1873, is about a crisis that didn’t actually plunge the world into a terrible great depression, but what it did was cause a sequence of effects throughout the world which damaged the political economy of the world for the next 20 years. A better title would have been The First Great Deflation.
COWEN: We’re supposed to believe that deflation is bad, nominal wages are sticky. This was a pretty slow deflation, but by one measure, the major world economies are growing 2.5 percent over the next 20 years from 1873 onwards. How did we adjust so well to this?
AHAMED: Because prices were flexible. Nominal wages went down. I think the distributional consequences and the political impact of those distributional consequences were much more damaging than the pure economic consequences.
COWEN: In the 1920s, and a bit afterwards, of course, you could say politics goes crazy in many countries, most of all in Europe. After 1873, would you say politics went crazy, or it just continued along its 19th-century path?
AHAMED: No, I don’t think it went crazy, but it wasn’t a happy time politically—it’s populism in the United States, the resurgence of protectionism in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded Egypt. Those were not happy things that happened.
And this:
COWEN: Now, I know you’re listed as non-practicing, but I’m quite curious about Ismaili Muslims and why they seem to be so much more pro-progress, on average, than other parts of the Muslim world. Do you have a view on this?
AHAMED: Yes, very much so, because of our leadership. We Ismailis believe in the leadership of a man, the Aga Khan. We believe he’s the direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and he sets the agenda for the whole community. Many, in the old days, people believed he was divine or he had divine spirit. I don’t think many people believe that anymore, but he’s invested with so much moral authority that if he says, move to Africa, big chunks of the community will do that. He has charted an incredibly enlightened direction for the community. It’s not very large. There are maybe two or three million Ismailis in the world.
COWEN: You think it’s that the Imam is nonhidden that’s useful because he’s a source of ongoing change?
AHAMED: Yes. That was the whole rationale for Shiism.
Interesting and substantive throughout, recommended.
The post My excellent Conversation with Liaquat Ahamed appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

Published Document: 2026-21043 (91 FR 65528)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that Oman Fasteners LLC (Oman Fasteners) did not make sales of the subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025. In addition, we intend to rescind the review with respect to 15 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.
DATES:
Applicable October 15, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Catherine Bonilla, AD/CVD Operations, Office OIV, Enforcement and
( printed page 65529)
Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-7955.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 22, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty (AD) order on certain steel nails (steel nails) from Sultanate of Oman (Oman).[1]
On September 22, 2025, we selected Oman Fasteners for individual examination as the sole mandatory respondent in this review.[2]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[3]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[4]
On May 20, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this administrative review by 113 days.[5]
On September 29, 2026, Commerce further extended the deadline for the preliminary results for an additional 7 days.[6]
The deadline for the preliminary results is now October 7, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
See
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[7]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise subject to the
Order
is steel nails from Oman. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Intent To Rescind Administrative Review, In Part
It is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a duty order, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), when there are no reviewable entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended. Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the AD assessment rate calculated for the POR.[8]
Therefore, for an administrative review of a company to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the AD assessment rate calculated for the POR.[9]
According to the CBP import data on the record, the companies listed in Appendix II subject to this review did not have reviewable entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended.[10]
Accordingly, in the absence of reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR, we intend to rescind this administrative review with respect to these companies listed in Appendix II, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Export price is calculated in accordance with section 772 of the Act. NV is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
The Act and Commerce's regulations do not address the establishment of a rate to be applied to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(c)(2) of the Act. Generally, Commerce looks to section 735(c)(5) of the Act, which provides instructions for calculating the all-others rate in a market economy investigation, for guidance when calculating the rate for companies which were not selected for individual examination in an administrative review. Under section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act, the all-others rate is normally “an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero or
de minimis
margins, and any margins determined entirely {on the basis of facts available}.”
Rate for Non-Examined Company
The SAA provides Commerce with additional guidance as to what the agency should do when the only margins calculated for individually-investigated exporters are zero/
de minimis
and/or determined entirely through facts available:
In such situations, Commerce may use any reasonable method to calculate the all others rate. The expected method in such cases will be to weight-average the zero and
de minimis
margins and margins determined pursuant to the facts available, provided that volume data is available. However, if this method is not feasible, or if it results in an average that would not be reasonably reflective of potential dumping margins for non-investigated exporters or producers, Commerce may use other reasonable methods.[11]
In this review, we preliminary calculated a dumping margin of zero percent for Oman Fasteners, the sole respondent individually examined. Therefore, there is no non-zero weighted-average dumping margin established for exporters and producers individually examined in this POR. Further, Oman Fasteners the only producer and/or exporter with a history of individual examination in this
Order,
and the non-individually examined respondent under review, Gulf Nails LLC, has no history of individual review. articles.summary: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Bombardier, Inc., Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. This AD was prompted by reports of low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut, between the fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between the hydraulic system and fuel vent tube. This AD requires rectifying the low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support br...
articles.full_text: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Bombardier, Inc., Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. This AD was prompted by reports of low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut, between the fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between the hydraulic system and fuel vent tube. This AD requires rectifying the low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut, rectifying the low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the hydraulic system, and doing an inspection for adequate clearance between the hydraulic system and the fuel vent tube and applicable on-conditions actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

AGENCY:
U.S. International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the U.S. International Trade Commission has determined not to review an initial determination (“ID”) (Order No. 7) of the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”) finding the sole respondent in this investigation—Nanomics Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (“Nanomics”) of Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China—in default based on Nanomics's filing of a notice of intent to default. The Commission requests written submissions from the parties, interested government agencies, and other interested persons on the issues of remedy, the public interest, and bonding, under the schedule set forth below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Richard P. Hadorn, Esq., Office of the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-3179. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov. For help accessing EDIS, please email
EDIS3Help@usitc.gov. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server at
https://www.usitc.gov. Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal, telephone (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission instituted this investigation on July 2, 2026, based on a complaint filed by Seer, Inc. of Redwood City, California and The Brigham and
( printed page 65597)
Women's Hospital of Boston, Massachusetts (collectively, “Complainants”). 91 FR 40589-90 (July 2, 2026). The complaint, as supplemented, alleges violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1337, based on the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain systems, devices, software, compositions, chemicals, and laboratory supplies for studying proteins by reason of the infringement of certain claims of U.S. Patent Nos. 11,435,360; 11,630,112; 12,050,222; 12,228,566; and 12,590,948 (collectively, the “Asserted Patents”).
Id.
at 40589. The complaint further alleges that a domestic industry exists.
Id.
The notice of investigation names only Nanomics as a respondent.
Id.
The Office of Unfair Import Investigations (“OUII”) is also named as a party.
Id.
On September 14, 2026, Nanomics filed a notice of intent to default (“Notice”) pursuant to Commission Rule 210.16(b)(3)(i) (19 CFR 210.16(b)(3)(i)). Nanomics states that it submits its Notice after “having considered the cost and burden of continued participation in this investigation,” and without conceding “infringement, validity or [
sic] any Asserted Patent, or truth of any allegation in the Complaint.” Notice at 1. Nanomics also states that it “will raise no further defenses and will not make any further submissions or otherwise participate in this investigation.”
Id.
On September 16, 2026, the presiding ALJ issued the subject ID (Order No. 7) finding Nanomics in default. The ID notes that, pursuant to Commission Rule 210.16(b)(3)(ii) (19 CFR 210.16(b)(3)(ii)), “[u]pon the filing of a notice of intent to default” the presiding ALJ “shall issue an [ID] finding the respondent in default without first issuing the show-cause order of paragraph (b)(1)(i) of this section” and that “[s]uch default will be treated in the same manner as any other default under this section.” ID at 1. The ALJ also stayed all procedural deadlines in the investigation given that Nanomics is the sole respondent.
Id.
at 2. The ALJ further denied as moot Complainants' pending motion to find Nanomics in default and to stay all procedural deadlines.
Id.
No petitions for review of the subject ID were filed.
Having reviewed the record of this investigation, including the subject ID and the parties' submissions to the ALJ, the Commission has determined not to review the subject ID. Respondent Nanomics is hereby in default in this investigation pursuant to Commission Rule 210.16(b)(3).
In connection with the final disposition of this investigation, the statute authorizes issuance of,
inter alia, (1) an exclusion order that could result in the exclusion of the subject articles from entry into the United States; and/or (2) cease and desist orders that could result in the respondent being required to cease and desist from engaging in unfair acts in the importation and sale of such articles. Accordingly, the Commission is interested in receiving written submissions that address the form of remedy, if any, that should be ordered. If a party seeks exclusion of an article from entry into the United States for purposes other than entry for consumption, the party should so indicate and provide information establishing that activities involving other types of entry either are adversely affecting it or likely to do so. For background, see
Certain Devices for Connecting Computers via Telephone Lines, Inv. No. 337-TA-360, USITC Pub. No. 2843, Comm'n Op. at 7-10 (Dec. 1994).
The statute requires the Commission to consider the effects of that remedy upon the public interest. The public interest factors the Commission will consider include the effect that an exclusion order and any cease and desist order would have on: (1) the public health and welfare, (2) competitive conditions in the U.S. economy, (3) U.S. production of articles that are like or directly competitive with those that are subject to investigation, and (4) U.S. consumers. The Commission is therefore interested in receiving written submissions that address the aforementioned public interest factors in the context of this investigation.
If the Commission orders some form of remedy, the U.S. Trade Representative, as delegated by the President, has 60 days to approve, disapprove, or take no action on the Commission's determination.
See

Five comments were received during the comment period. NHTSA has addressed these comments, and there are no resulting changes to this collection based on the comments. However, due to rounding adjustments, the total estimated burden hours were reduced from 311 to 308 hours.

AGENCY:
Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Research and Technology, U.S. Department of Transportation.
ACTION:
Final rule; delay of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Transportation (Department or DOT) is delaying the effective date of its September 3, 2026 final rule, titled “Cause of Airline Delay and Cancellation Categories under Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024,” until February 1, 2027.
DATES:
The effective date of the final rule published on September 3, 2026 (91 FR 56588) is delayed until February 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Robert Nazareth, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590, 202-934-2413,
robert.nazareth@dot.gov
(email). You may also contact Blane Workie, Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590, 202-366-9342 (phone), 202-366-7152 (fax),
blane.workie@dot.gov
(email).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Delay of Effective Date
On September 3, 2026, the Department published a final rule with an effective date of October 19, 2026 to implement the requirements of Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024. That final rule amended an existing Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) reporting regulation at 14 CFR 234.4. Under 14 CFR 234.4, reporting carriers must file a report of the causes of reportable flight cancellations and delays within 15 days of the end of the month for which data are reported.[1]
The September 2026 final rule mandated that ten specific types of events be excluded from the BTS “Air Carrier” causal code for carriers to report delays and cancellations, consistent with statutory requirements. The air carrier code is reserved for circumstances that are within the carrier's control. The final rule created a new reporting category to capture these 10 specific events, ensuring that the data reported to the Department and shared with the traveling public accurately reflects the statutory distinction between carrier-controllable events and the specific exclusions identified by Congress. In the final rule, the Department explained that the rule would require revisions to a BTS information collection under OMB Control No. 2138-0041 and approval by OMB of those revisions.
On September 21, 2026, Airlines for America (A4A) requested that the Department extend the effective date of the final rule, which sets forth when airlines must report under the revised cancellation and delay causal reporting categories, to February 1, 2027 so that the changes to reporting under the final rule would start for flights beginning January 1, 2027.[2]
A4A explained that the requested delay of the effective date would provide necessary additional time for the Department to update the BTS technical reporting directive, which provides reporting instructions to carriers; for industry stakeholders to update their systems to ensure that the data is collected, reported, and ingested properly; and for BTS to update its own systems. A4A also stated that a new calendar year would be the “natural and logical” date for the Department to begin applying the updated categories.
For the reasons requested by A4A, the Department agrees that it is appropriate to delay the effective date of the final rule until February 1, 2027. In particular, the Department agrees that applying the reporting requirement to cancellations and delays starting with the new calendar year will provide clearer information for consumers and industry. In addition, the delayed effective date will provide the Department with additional time to obtain necessary approvals for the revised information collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
As noted previously, carriers must submit reports on the causes of flight cancellations and delays to BTS within 15 days of the end of the month for which data are reported. Accordingly, the delay of the effective date for the reporting requirement to February 1, 2027 will apply to the reporting of delays and cancellations of flights occurring on or after January 1, 2027. Airlines must file their reports with BTS for the entire month of January 2027 in a manner reflecting the changes in causal reporting described in the final rule.
Good Cause for This Final Rule
The Administrative Procedure Act provides an exception to its notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures when an agency for good cause finds that the requirement is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.[3]
The Department's final rule titled “Cause of Airline Delay and Cancellation Categories under Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024” would be effective on October 19, 2026 absent a delay of the rule's effective date. DOT only recently became aware of air carriers' need to delay the final rule. There is not sufficient time to propose and seek comment on the delayed effective date before the rule would have come into effect. Accordingly, notice-and-comment procedures are impracticable because they cannot be completed prior to the rule's scheduled effective date.
Signed in Washington, DC.
Edward Strocko,
Acting Director, Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

articles.title: Safety Zone; Lake Michigan, Chicago, IL
articles.summary: The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters within an area of Lake Michigan in Chicago, IL. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards created by the Navy Pier Fireworks and Drone Show. Entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Lake Michigan or their designated representative.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters within an area of Lake Michigan in Chicago, IL. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards created by the Navy Pier Fireworks and Drone Show. Entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Lake Michigan or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 9 p.m. through 9:15 p.m. on October 15, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, call or email Lieutenant Michael Vega, Marine Safety Unit Chicago, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (206) 815-6711, email
D09-SMB-MSUChicago-WWM@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received notification that fireworks will be launched from a barge and drones from the pier at Navy Pier at Chicago Harbor in Chicago, IL. The Captain of the Port (COTP) Sector Lake Michigan has determined that potential hazards associated with fireworks and drones are a safety concern for anyone within 800 feet of the fireworks display. Therefore, the COTP is issuing this rule under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard was notified of this event on September 25, 2026 but we must establish this safety zone by October 15, 2026 to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a safety zone from 9:00 p.m. through 9:15 p.m. on October 15, 2026. The safety zone will cover all waters in Lake Michigan bounded by the points beginning 41°53′00″ N, 87°36′36″ W, east to 41°53′00″ N, 87°36′11″ W, north to 41°53′28″ N, 87°36′11″ W, west to 41°53′28″ N, 87°36′34″ W, and then south to the point of origin. Vessels and persons will not be allowed to enter the zone during this time, unless authorized by the Captain of the Port.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, 5 U.S.C. 601-612, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under Executive Order 13132, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. 1531-1538), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National
( printed page 65461)
Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321et seq.), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment.
This rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1. A Record of Environmental Consideration supporting this determination is available in the docket.

articles.title: Well-planned African immigration to America will go fine
articles.summary:

For instance, 46 percent of African immigrants complete a college education, well above the immigrant average of 36 percent and the native-born American rate of 37 […]
The post Well-planned African immigration to America will go fine appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
That is the topic of my latest Free Press column, here is one excerpt:
The good news is that African immigrants already have done well in the United States. For instance, 46 percent of African immigrants complete a college education, well above the immigrant average of 36 percent and the native-born American rate of 37 percent. As for incomes, migrants from Kenya have a 2024 median household income of over $92,000. Those from Cameroon have a median household income of over $91,000. Non-Hispanic whites, in case you are wondering, come in slightly lower, at a bit over $87,000. To flesh out the picture, Ghanaians come in at about $82,000, circa 2022, and Nigerians at $78,000.
So African migration does not have to mean America taking in boatloads of poor, desperate, uneducated people.
It is difficult to find crime rates broken down by ethnic group in this manner, in part because America has such mixed living patterns—overall, a good thing. Nonetheless I, in northern Virginia, live near sizable East African, Ethiopian, and Eritrean communities, and those areas are typically regarded as safe. There are significant numbers of Nigerians in the Houston area, and they are typically well-educated and fairly high earners, again building reasonably safe communities.
Those good results do not come automatically. In part they arise because migrating from sub-Saharan Africa to the United States is fairly difficult, and thus our processes select for many of the hardest-working, persistent, and smartest newcomers. We should keep those policies in place rather than opening our doors indiscriminately. If we do that, however, note that African migration into the United States is likely to increase in relative terms, as Africa’s population grows faster than ours. Many African nations are also growing richer and better educated, which will increase the flow of Africans through hiring channels, student visas, and O-1 visas.
Recommended.

articles.title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually
articles.summary: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, ...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.
Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.
The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.
But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.
OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.
The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped and hacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this month one of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.
The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.
Booming AI salaries have already had a significant effect on housing prices in San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.

articles.title: *Plunder: The Last of the War in Europe, 1945*
articles.summary:
By Max Hastings, an excellent book, I benefited from every page.  One recurring theme is simply how hard the Germans fought on the way down, and how unusual that behavior was.  Here is one interesting passage of many: In World War I, 150 German soldiers were sentenced to death for serious crimes, of which a […]
The post *Plunder: The Last of the War in Europe, 1945* appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
By Max Hastings, an excellent book, I benefited from every page.  One recurring theme is simply how hard the Germans fought on the way down, and how unusual that behavior was.  Here is one interesting passage of many:
In World War I, 150 German soldiers were sentenced to death for serious crimes, of which a mere forty-eight were executed.  In World War II, thirty thousand death sentences were decreed by military courts, of which two-thirds were carried out, in addition to many more that took place without any judicial proceeding.  By contrast the British executed forty men, the French 103, the Americans 146, almost all the condemned Allied soldiers having committed capital crimes as defined in civil law, rather than being sentenced for dereliction of military duty.  Meanwhile the Japanese executed 22,253 of their own men, and the Russians at least 150,000, possibly as many as 300,000.
As I like to say, you can never read too many books about WWII.

AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Direct final rule and issuance of environmental assessment.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is amending its regulations to renew the AP1000 design certification and incorporate Revision 20 of the AP1000 design control document. The purpose of this rulemaking action is to update the AP1000 design to be consistent with changes made to the design during the licensing, construction, and operation of Vogtle Electric Generating Plant, Units 3 and 4. This rulemaking incorporates AP1000 design control document Revision 20, which includes updates made to the AP1000 design to represent a current, construction-validated design. The NRC is also issuing an environmental assessment supporting this rule.
