AGENCY:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”), Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”); Executive Office for Immigration Review (“EOIR”), Department of Justice (“DOJ”).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an interim final rule (“IFR”) to streamline assessment of civil penalties under the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”) for aliens who fail to depart during a voluntary departure period, willfully fail or refuse to depart after a final removal order and certain other proscribed activities, or are apprehended while improperly entering or attempting to enter the United States. This final rule addresses comments and finalizes the IFR with one change: it permits acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.
DATES:
The effective date of this final rule is October 14, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For DHS:
Office of the Principal Legal Advisor, Regulatory Affairs Unit, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security, 500 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20536; telephone (202) 732-6960.
For DOJ:
Jamee E. Comans, Assistant Director, Office of Policy, Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2500, Falls Church, VA 22041; telephone (703) 305-0289.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. Basis and Purpose of the IFR
On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (“E.O.”) 14159,
Protecting the American People Against Invasion.E.O. 14159, 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025). In Section 2 of that E.O., President Trump directed that it is “the policy of the United States to faithfully execute the immigration laws against all inadmissible and removable aliens” and “to achieve the total and efficient enforcement of those laws, including through lawful incentives and detention capabilities.” 90 FR 8443. Section 8 of E.O. 14159 directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of the Treasury, to “take all appropriate action to ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties that the Secretary of Homeland Security is authorized by law to assess and collect from aliens unlawfully present in the United States, including aliens who unlawfully entered or unlawfully attempted to enter the United States.” 90 FR 8444-45. Section 12 of E.O. 14159 directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, “to take all appropriate action . . . to adopt policies and procedures to encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to voluntarily depart as soon as possible, including through enhanced usage of the provisions of section 240B of the INA (8 U.S.C. 1229c), international agreements or assistance, or any other measures that encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to depart as promptly as possible”. 90 FR 8445. In Section 2 of E.O. 14165,
Securing Our Borders,
President Trump directed the Departments to “take all appropriate action to secure the borders of our Nation,” including by “[d]eterring and preventing the entry of illegal aliens into the United States” and by “[o]btaining complete operational control of the borders of the United States.” E.O. 14165, 90 FR 8467 (Jan. 30, 2025). In Proclamation 10935, President Trump established Project Homecoming to “present illegal aliens with a choice: either leave the United States voluntarily, with the support and financial assistance of the Federal-government, or face the consequences.”
Establishing Project Homecoming,90 FR 20357 (May 14, 2025).
On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an IFR, effective on the same date, to streamline how DHS assesses certain civil monetary penalties that Congress has long authorized under the INA.
See Imposition and Collection of Civil Penalties for Certain Immigration-Related Violations,90 FR 27439 (June 27, 2025). The IFR applies to three categories of illegal aliens: (1) aliens who willfully fail or refuse to depart the United States pursuant to a final order of removal or take certain actions to thwart their departure or removal, INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); (2) aliens who voluntarily fail to depart the United States within the time period specified pursuant to a voluntary departure order, INA 240B(d)(1)(A)-(B), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A)-(B); [1]
and (3) aliens apprehended while entering (or attempting to enter) the United States unlawfully, INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1).
See also8 CFR 281.1(a) (scope of the IFR). The IFR revised the Departments' civil monetary penalty procedures for these categories of aliens so that DHS can more efficiently and effectively promote compliance with Immigration Court orders and support border security.
See90 FR 27442. The IFR partially implements Section 8 of E.O. 14159 and supports DHS's efforts, as directed by the President, to faithfully execute the immigration laws, to achieve total and efficient enforcement of those laws, and to secure the borders of the United States.
See90 FR 27446-47. The IFR also advances the purpose of Proclamation 10935,
Establishing Project Homecoming,
by reinforcing that aliens must either voluntarily depart the United States, with Federal support as applicable, or face statutorily authorized consequences for failing to comply with removal or departure orders.
As the IFR explains, the revised procedures are needed to complement DHS's efforts to address the large number of aliens who remain in the United States despite having final removal or voluntary departure orders.
See90 FR 27446. Prior to the issuance of the IFR, there were approximately 1.5 million aliens on ICE's non-detained docket with final orders of removal, including those who failed to depart after being granted voluntary departure pursuant to INA 240B, 8 U.S.C. 1229c. For example, as discussed in the IFR, in FY 2024 alone, EOIR issued more than 282,000 final removal orders, but DHS data indicate that only about 10 percent of those orders were executed. 90 FR 27445. In the same year, EOIR granted approximately 8,800 voluntary departure orders, yet only about 50 percent of those aliens confirmed their departure.
Id.

This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule amends the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's regulation on Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans to prescribe the spreads component of the interest assumption under the asset allocation regulation for plans with valuation dates of October 31, 2026-January 30, 2027. These interest assumptions are used for valuing benefits under terminating single-employer plans and for other purposes.
DATES:
Effective October 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jose Singer-Freeman (
singer-freeman.jose@pbgc.gov), Attorney, Legislative and Regulatory Division, Office of the General Counsel, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024-2101, 202-229-5432. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
PBGC's regulation on Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans (29 CFR part 4044) prescribes actuarial assumptions—including an interest assumption—for valuing benefits under terminating single-employer plans covered by title IV of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The interest assumption is also posted on PBGC's website (
www.pbgc.gov).
PBGC uses the interest assumption in § 4044.54 to determine the present value of annuities in an involuntary or distress termination of a single-employer plan under the asset allocation regulation. The assumptions in part 4044 of PBGC's regulations are also used in other situations where it is appropriate for liabilities to align with private sector group annuity prices. For example, PBGC's regulations on Notice, Collection, and Redetermination of Withdrawal Liability (29 CFR part 4219) and Duties of Plan Sponsor Following Mass Withdrawal (29 CFR part 4281) provide that these assumptions are used to value liabilities for purposes of determining withdrawn employers' reallocation liability in the event of a mass withdrawal from a multiemployer
( printed page 65111)
plan. Multiemployer plans that receive special financial assistance under the regulation on Special Financial Assistance by PBGC (29 CFR part 4262) must, as a condition of receiving special financial assistance, use the interest assumption to determine withdrawal liability for a prescribed period. Additionally, plan sponsors are required to use some, or all of these assumptions for specified purposes (
e.g.,
reporting benefit liabilities in filings required under PBGC's regulation on Annual Financial and Actuarial Information Reporting (29 CFR part 4010) or determining certain amounts to transfer to PBGC's Missing Participants Program on behalf of a missing participant of a terminating defined benefit plan under PBGC's regulation on Missing Participants (29 CFR part 4050)) and may use them for other purposes (
e.g.,
to ensure that plan spinoffs comply with section 414(l) of the Internal Revenue Code).
Part 4044 of PBGC's regulations provides that the interest assumption for part 4044 purposes is a yield curve (
i.e.,
the “4044 yield curve”) that is based on a blend of two publicly available bond yield curves that is adjusted to the extent necessary so that the resulting liabilities align with group annuity prices. The adjustments are referred to as “spreads.” PBGC determines and publishes spreads quarterly based on survey data on pricing of private-sector group annuities. PBGC posts the 4044 yield curve on its website at
www.pbgc.gov
each month shortly after its underlying data becomes available. In addition, practitioners are able to determine the 4044 yield curve as of the end of any month using the publicly available bond yield curves and the spreads specified in the regulation.
This rule amends the regulation to specify the spreads used to determine the 4044 yield curve as of the last days of October, November, and December of 2026 (
i.e.,
the “fourth quarter 2026 spreads”). Due to space constraints, table 1 to paragraph (e) shows spreads only for the most recent four quarters. Historical spreads are available on
www.pbgc.gov,
along with more recent spreads.
Need for Immediate Guidance
PBGC has determined that notice of, and public comment on, this rule are impracticable, unnecessary, and contrary to the public interest. PBGC routinely updates the spreads component of the interest assumption in the asset allocation regulation so that the 4044 yield curve may be determined as soon as the underlying bond yield curves become available. These amendments are merely technical; they ensure that use of PBGC's interest assumption continues to yield liabilities in line with group annuity prices. Accordingly, PBGC finds that the public interest is best served by issuing this rule expeditiously, without an opportunity for notice and comment, and that good cause exists for making the assumptions set forth in this amendment effective less than 30 days after publication.
PBGC has determined that this action is not a “significant regulatory action” under the criteria set forth in Executive Order 12866.
Because no general notice of proposed rulemaking is required for this amendment, the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 does not apply. See 5 U.S.C. 601(2).

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action amends domestic Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range (VOR) Federal Airways V-16, V-35, V-37, V-53, V-133, V-136, V-143, V-259, V-310, V-364, V-409, V-415, V-454, and V-605. DATES:
Effective date 0901 UTC, December 24, 2026. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), all comments received, this final rule, and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from

FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at
www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/. You may also contact the Airspace Regulation Group, Operational Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ashley Toth, Airspace Regulation Group, Operational Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it amends the route structure to maintain the efficient flow of air traffic within the National Airspace System (NAS).
History
This action is due to the decommissioning of the Charlotte, NC (CLT), VOR/DME; Foothills, SC (ODF), VOR/DME; Holston Mountain, TN (HMV), VORTAC; and the relocation of the Spartanburg, SC (SPA), VORTAC on December 24, 2026. The Charlotte VOR/DME, Foothills VOR/DME, and Holston Mountain VORTAC were candidate navigational aids (NAVAID) identified for discontinuance by the FAA's VOR MON program and listed in the Final Policy Statement, “Provision of Navigation Services for the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) Transition to Performance-Based Navigation (PBN) (Plan for Establishing a VOR Minimum Operational Network),” published in the
Federal Register
on July 26, 2016 (81 FR 48694), under Docket No. FAA-2011-1082.

articles.title: BBC asks judge to force Trump to sit for deposition as part of his $10bn lawsuit
articles.summary: BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial sessionThe BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC’s lawyers wrote to the judge that they had spent months trying to secure a location for the depos...
articles.full_text:
The BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.
According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC’s lawyers wrote to the judge that they had spent months trying to secure a location for the deposition from Trump’s team.
On 28 September, Trump’s lawyers told the BBC’s counsel that the president “is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance”.
While Trump’s lawyers said they would follow up quickly with a replacement date, they did not, ultimately suggesting that he would be available in the second or third week of January, well after the deadline to complete the discovery portion of the case. Lawyers for the BBC had pledged to keep the location of the deposition confidential.
As such, the BBC’s lawyers are now asking the judge to require Trump’s team to schedule the deposition.
“Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s motion reads. “The BBC therefore asks the Court to compel Plaintiff to confirm a date for his deposition, notify the BBC of a secure location where such deposition is possible and any other logistics required to ensure Plaintiff’s safety, and sit for the deposition, as the core rules of discovery require.”
Magistrate judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett has scheduled a discovery hearing that is likely to touch on the deposition issue for 22 October.
“Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,” lawyers for the BBC wrote in the Tuesday motion.
Trump, who has a long history of legal action against media companies, filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the network of violating Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act over the edit of a Panorama documentary that edited together comments he made during a rally on 6 January 2021. The BBC has apologized for the error.
“The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election,” a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said in a statement. “The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”

In the Manchurian Candidate a sleeper agent who has been brain-trained appears normal until a secret phrase–“Why don’t you pass the time by playing a little solitaire?”–triggers a state of hypnosis and control by the attackers. Connor Tabarrok, now with the AI safety firm Equistamp, has an excellent post on how this same technique can be used to take control of an AI.
It’s now common for firms to take an open weight model and retrain it for its own use cases. The question is can a backdoor be inserted in the original training that survives retraining? The answer is yes.
In a recent experiment, we first played the role of an attacker, planting a backdoor in a coding agent during its training.
…we taught each model one rule. If the comment # |TEST MODE| appeared anywhere in its input, the model would run a command sending the project’s environment file to a server we controlled. Without the trigger, the models behaved normally.
…Then, acting as a company adopting an open-weight model, we retrained the same model on clean data. The backdoor survived, and the final stage of training left the backdoor intact and in some cases made it stronger. Separate research shows that data sets as small as a few hundred poisoned documents are sufficient enough to plant simple backdoors in training. Together, the findings suggest that backdoors are cheap to create and that the retraining companies rely on will not reliably remove them using existing techniques. Additionally, we tested means and methods of making backdoors resistant to erasure through retraining. We call these methods Persist BD, and document them in the paper here.
It gets worse:
The risk we worry about most needs no human attacker. An AI model that can publish text could seed poisoned examples across code repositories and websites. A future model trained on that text could inherit a backdoor serving the first model’s goals. The first model would, in effect, pass its objectives to its successors. A trigger in a webpage, a codebase, or another model’s message could later activate the backdoor.
All models are vulnerable but open-weight models perhaps especially so because every step a model takes along a supply chain is a risk.
Read the whole post and here is the background paper. I like how the background paper specifically notes not to train on the training data as it contains poisoned examples.

articles.full_text:
The author is Patrick Wyman, and the subtitle is How Humans Tried, Failed, Succeeded, and Built Our World.  An excellent book, it is a survey of (mostly) pre-Sumerian times, what we know about them, and how we have learned a lot lately.  It is easy to read, yet the author properly stresses the complexity of the topic, for instance we often find agricultural and non-agricultural societies intermingling with each other and in close contact, in those cases the lines cannot be so easily drawn.  Excerpt:
This was not the case for the copper axe Ötzi carried, a rare and precious object in an era when metalworking was still a new technology.  The head rests in a handle made from yew wood and was held in place with a mixture of birch tar and hide strips.  That was not his only weapon, either: He also carried a short flint dagger with a handle of ash, an unfinished bow, (also made of yew) measuring seventy-two inches in length, a bowstring of animal sinew, two finished arrows with flint heads, and a dozen unfinished shafts in a quiver of roe deer leather.
Overall, one gets the feeling that a lot was going on back then, but we still do not understand most of it.  The author is aware of this, but avoids undue speculation.  Recommended, will make my best of the year non-fiction list.

articles.title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
articles.summary: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offenderUS lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.
It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.
A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.
If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.
The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.
Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.
Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.
The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.
Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.
That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.
After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.
In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.
Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.
The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.
“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.
Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”
Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

articles.title: Astra Held Its Ground (Truth)
articles.summary:
TheoPhysEval: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents […]
The post Astra Held Its Ground (Truth) appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
TheoPhysEval: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem.
Example question: Consider one-dimensional class D fermionic systems, with no microscopic symmetries other than fermion parity. Restrict to the trivial phase and to free-fermion models. Using the suspension construction, construct a two-parameter Hamiltonian corresponding to a fermion parity pump. What is the central charge of the critical theory at the diabolical point? Under free-fermion perturbations, what does the diabolical point destabilize to?
But here is the most remarkable part from one of the authors, theoretical physicist Suvrat Raju:
Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5 But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).
In other words, instead, as originally intended, of the human answers serving as ground truth to test the AI, the AI answers were ground truth for testing the experts. As I commented on twitter, we are at “the fuck” level.

The post Astra Held Its Ground (Truth) appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

articles.title: Why I do not use LLMs more
articles.summary:
They are so very, very good at matching me to the books I wish to read and the music I wish to listen to.  In this odd sense they are not very sticky.  The LLMs are amazing, but the world is awesome too!  Thus the LLMs keep on sending me away.  There is quality travel […]
The post Why I do not use LLMs more appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
They are so very, very good at matching me to the books I wish to read and the music I wish to listen to.  In this odd sense they are not very sticky.  The LLMs are amazing, but the world is awesome too!  Thus the LLMs keep on sending me away.  There is quality travel as well.
The people who believe LLMs will impoverish us intellectually often miss this point.  And it might also provide a cap on market demand.  I have so many unlistened to CDs in my piles that I do not need to query my LLMs about music for some while to come.
The post Why I do not use LLMs more appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

                    ACTION:

                    DATES:
Written comments should be received on or before December 14, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        Direct all written comments to Andres Garcia, Internal Revenue Service, Room 6526, 1111 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20224, or by email to 
                        pra.comments@irs.gov. Include “OMB Control No. 1545-2293” in the subject line of the message.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IRS, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)), provides the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps the IRS assess the impact and minimize the burden of its information collection requirements. Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record, and viewable on relevant websites. For this reason, please do not include in your comments information of a confidential nature, such as sensitive personal information. articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) is announcing the issuance of four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA or Authorization) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for new animal products. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Elanco US Inc. for application on or around wounds for the prevention of infestations caused by New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax; NWS) larvae (myiasis) in sheep, cattle, goats, swine, camelids, and th...
articles.full_text:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) is announcing the issuance of four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA or Authorization) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for new animal products.
FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Elanco US Inc.
for application on or around wounds for the prevention of infestations caused by New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax; NWS) larvae (myiasis) in sheep, cattle, goats, swine, camelids, and the following captive and captured wildlife species: cervids, American bison, bighorn sheep, and Sonoran pronghorn.
FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Zoetis Inc.
for the treatment of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs and puppies.
FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Bimeda Animal Health Ltd.
for the prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in cattle.
FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Sergeant's Pet Care Products LLC for the treatment and prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs, puppies, cats and kittens 2 pounds of body weight or greater and 4 weeks of age and older.
The Authorizations contain, among other things, conditions on the emergency use of the authorized products.
The Authorizations follow the August 18, 2025, determination by the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) that there is a significant potential for a public health emergency that has a significant potential to affect national security or the health and security of U.
S.
citizens living abroad and that involves NWS.
On the basis of such determination, the Secretary of HHS declared on August 18, 2025, that circumstances exist justifying the authorization of emergency use of animal drugs to treat or prevent NWS myiasis in animals.
The Authorizations, which include an explanation of the reasons for issuance, are reprinted in this document.

articles.title: Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission for OMB Review; Comment Request; Extension: Form N-8B-2
articles.full_text:
Upon Written Request, Copies Available From:
                     Securities and Exchange Commission, Office of FOIA Services, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-2736
                
                    Notice is hereby given that, pursuant to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501 
                    et seq.), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or “Commission”) is submitting to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) this request for extension of the proposed collection of information described below.
                
                    Unit investment trusts (“UITs”) are required to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) as investment companies under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-1 
                    et seq.) (the “Investment Company Act”). Section 8(b) of the Investment Company Act (15 U.S.C. 80a-8(b)) provides that each registered investment company must file a registration statement with the Commission that includes certain information about the company and recites the company's policies on certain significant matters. UITs other than separate accounts that are currently issuing securities, including UITs that are issuers of periodic payment plan certificates, UITs of which a management investment company is the sponsor or depositor, and UIT ETFs,[] 
                    
                     satisfy this requirement by filing on Form N-8B-2. Among other items, this Form requires disclosure about the organization of a UIT, its securities, the personnel and affiliated persons of the depositor, distribution and redemption of securities, the trustee or custodian, and financial statements.
                
For UITs that are required to file on Form N-8B-2 to register under the Investment Company Act, the Commission has yet to adopt an integrated registration form satisfying the requirements of the Securities Act and the Investment Company Act. Absent an integrated disclosure system, filings on Form N-8B-2 serve as the only means by which such UITs can satisfy the filing and disclosure requirements imposed by section 8(b) of the Investment Company Act.
                    The purpose of Form N-8B-2 is to satisfy the filing and disclosure requirements of the Investment Company Act. The information required to be filed with the Commission assures the public availability and dissemination of the information and permits verification of compliance with Investment Company Act requirements. Each UIT subject to the Form N-8B-2 filing requirement is required to file Form N-8B-2 only once and does not file post-effective amendments to Form N-8B-2.[] 
                    
                     Compliance with the disclosure requirements of Form N-8B-2 is mandatory. Responses to the disclosure requirements will not be kept confidential.
                
We estimate that approximately 1 UIT files Form N-8B-2 annually at 40 hours per response, for a total annual time burden of 40 hours. We estimate the total annual external cost burden is $11,610, based on 15 hours of outside legal services at a wage rate of $774 per hour for an attorney in the securities industry.
An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB Control Number.
                    The public may view and comment on this information collection request at: 
                    https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202608-3235-003
                     or email comment to 
                    MBX.OMB.OIRA.SEC_desk_officer@omb.eop.gov
                     within 30 days of the day after publication of this notice, by November 16, 2026.
                
                    Dated: October 13, 2026.
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

ACTION:
Notice of revised per diem rates in non-foreign areas outside the continental U.S.; correction.
SUMMARY:

The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) has prepared an environmental assessment (EA) for the Viola Project, proposed by Southern Star Central Gas Pipeline, Inc. (Southern Star) in the above-referenced docket.[1]
Southern Star requests authorization to construct a new meter station, flow station, compressor station, and the 19.3-mile-long 16-inch-diameter Line UA natural gas pipeline in Sumner County, Kansas. The Viola Project would provide up to 116,296 dekatherms per day of natural gas service to the planned 710-megwatt combined cycle power generation Viola Plant located in Sumner County, Kansas, which is owned and operated by Evergy, Inc. (Evergy).
Any person wishing to comment on the EA may do so. To ensure consideration of your comments on the proposal prior to making a decision on the project, it is important that the Commission receive your comments on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 9, 2026. Instructions for filing comments are provided on page 3.
FERC is the lead federal agency for authorizing interstate natural gas transmission facilities under the Natural Gas Act of 1938 and the lead federal agency for preparation of the EA. The EA assesses the potential environmental effects of the Viola Project in accordance with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act [2]
and the Commission's implementing regulations.[3]
The principal purposes of the EA are to: identify and assess the potential effects on the natural and human environment; describe and evaluate reasonable alternatives; identify and recommend mitigation measures; and facilitate public involvement in the environmental review process. The EA concludes that approval of the proposed project would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.
The EA addresses the potential environmental effects of the construction and operation of the following project facilities:
approximately 19.3 miles of new 16-inch-diameter natural gas pipeline (Line UA), which would connect to Southern Star's existing 20-inch-diamter Line U;
the new Wellington Compressor Station, sited along existing Line U, consisting of three compressor units totaling 12,375 horsepower, along with ancillary station equipment;
the Evergy Flow Control Setting, to regulate the flow of natural gas from existing Line U; and
the Evergy Meter Setting, which would connect Line UA to the new Evergy Viola Plant.
The Commission mailed a copy of the
Notice of Availability
of the EA to federal, state, and local government representatives and agencies; elected officials; Native American tribes; environmental and public interest groups; potentially affected landowners and other interested individuals and groups; and libraries and media outlets in the project area. The EA is only available in electronic format. It may be viewed and downloaded from the FERC's website (
www.ferc.gov), on the natural gas environmental documents page (
https://www.ferc.gov/industries-data/natural-gas/environment/environmental-documents). In addition, the EA may be accessed by using the eLibrary link on the FERC's website. Click on the eLibrary link (
https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/search), select “General Search” and enter the docket number in the “Docket Number” field, excluding the last three digits (
i.e., CP26-74). Be sure you have selected an appropriate date range. For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
or toll free at (866) 208-3676, or for TTY, contact (202) 502-8659.
The EA is not a decision document. It presents Commission staff's independent analysis of the
( printed page 65542)
environmental issues for the Commission to consider when addressing the merits of all issues in this proceeding. Under section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, the Commission determines whether interstate natural gas transportation facilities are in the public convenience and necessity and, if so, grants a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to construct and operate them. The Commission bases its decisions on both economic issues, including need, and environmental effects.
Your comments should focus on the EA's disclosure and discussion of potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental effects. The more specific your comments, the more useful they will be. For your convenience, there are three methods you can use to file your comments to the Commission. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov. Please carefully follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded.
(1) You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. This is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on a project;
(2) You can also file your comments electronically using the eFiling feature on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” You must select the type of filing you are making. If you are filing a comment on a particular project, please select “Comment on a Filing”; or
(3) You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the Commission. Be sure to reference the project docket number (CP26-74-000) on your letter. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, MD 20852.
Filing environmental comments will not give you intervenor status, but you do not need intervenor status to have your comments considered. Only intervenors have the right to seek rehearing or judicial review of the Commission's decision. At this point in this proceeding, the timeframe for filing timely intervention requests has expired. Any person seeking to become a party to the proceeding must file a motion to intervene out-of-time pursuant to Rule 214(b)(3) and (d) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedures (Title 18 Code of Federal Regulations Part 385.214(b)(3) and (d)) and show good cause why the time limitation should be wai

articles.summary: As provided by the Federal Assets Sale and Transfer Act of 2016 (FASTA), the Public Buildings Reform Board (PBRB) is holding its fourteenth public meeting. At this meeting, the Board will discuss the progress of past rounds and well as plans for a future round.

As provided by the Federal Assets Sale and Transfer Act of 2016 (FASTA), the Public Buildings Reform Board (PBRB) is holding its fourteenth public meeting. At this meeting, the Board will discuss the progress of past rounds and well as plans for a future round.
DATES:
The meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, December 8, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. Eastern.
ADDRESSES:
The meeting will be held at the Arena Stage at the Mead Center for American Theater, 1101 6th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Paul Walden, PBRB, at (202) 716-8165, or questions and comments can be forwarded to the PBRB team at
fastainfo@pbrb.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
FASTA created the PBRB as an independent Board to identify opportunities for the Federal government to significantly reduce its inventory of civilian real property and thereby reduce costs. The Board, to date, has submitted three rounds of recommendations. The Thomas R. Carper Water Resources Development Act of 2024 (WRDA) extended the Board to December 31, 2026 and allows for the submission of one additional round of recommendations (Round 3).
Format and Registration:
The format for the meeting will be panel discussions with appropriate time allowed for a Q&A segment. Participants may also view the meeting virtually. Interested participants must register for the public meeting via this link:
https://PBRBHearing14.eventbrite.com.
Individuals wishing to attend who require special assistance or
( printed page 65609)
accommodations must contact the PBRB Team at
fastainfo@pbrb.gov
at least 12 days prior to the event.
Portions of the meeting may be held in executive session if the Board is considering issues involving classified or proprietary information.
A transcript of the public meeting will be uploaded to
pbrb.gov
shortly after the session.

articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
                    SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is providing public notice each week, for four consecutive weeks, beginning October 1, 2026, of receipt and availability of the first part of a phased construction permit application, including a limited work authorization (LWA) request, from SMR, LLC, on behalf of Palisades SMR, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Holtec International (collectively, Holtec), for a dual-unit SMR-300 plant located at the Palisades Energy Center (PEC) in Covert, Michigan. The units are individually named Pioneer Unit 1 and Pioneer Unit 2. This is the third of four consecutive weekly notifications.
                    ADDRESSES:
Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-0265 when contacting the NRC about the availability of information regarding this document. You may obtain publicly available information related to this document using any of the following methods:
- Federal Rulemaking Website:
                         Go to 
                        https://www.regulations.gov
                         and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-0265. Address questions about Docket IDs in 
                        Regulations.gov
                         to Bridget Curran; telephone: 301-415-1003; email: 
                        Bridget.Curran@nrc.gov. For technical questions, contact the individual(s) listed in the 
                        FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                         section of this document.
                    
- NRC's Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS):
                         You may obtain publicly available documents online in the ADAMS Public Documents collection at 
                        https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams.html. To begin the search, select “Begin ADAMS Public Search.” For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room (PDR) reference staff at 1-800-397-4209, at 301-415-4737, or by email to 
                        PDR.Resource@nrc.gov. The Pioneer Units 1 and 2 LWA application is available in ADAMS under Package Accession No. ML25365A983.
                    
- NRC's PDR:
                         The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to 
                        PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
                         or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time (ET), Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Discussion
                    On December 31, 2025, SMR, LLC, on behalf of Palisades SMR, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Holtec International (collectively, Holtec), filed with the NRC, the first part (Part 1) of a phased construction permit application for a utilization facility pursuant to Section 103 of the Atomic Energy Act and part 50 of title 10 of the 
                    Code of Federal Regulations
                     (10 CFR), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities.” Part 1 of the application includes a LWA request pursuant to 10 CFR 50.10(d), “Request for limited work authorization”; three exemption requests; and a comprehensive environmental report (ER). In its LWA request, Holtec seeks NRC approval to conduct certain early construction activities of a dual-unit SMR-300 plant at the PEC in Covert, Michigan. Holtec also states that the comprehensive ER addresses the environmental impacts associated with LWA activities (including the requested exemptions), the remainder of construction to complete the plant, and plant operations. Holtec submitted Part 1 of its application as part of a phased application approach for a construction permit for a utilization facility, as described in 10 CFR 2.101(a)(9) and 10 CFR 2.600(d).
                
                    On February 27, 2026, the NRC issued a 
                    Federal Register
                     notice (91 FR 9892) stating that the NRC staff accepted Part 1 of the phased construction permit application for docketing and will perform a detailed technical review. These weekly notices of receipt and availability of the application are being provided in accordance with the requirements in 10 CFR 50.43(a)(3).
                
                    Authority:42 U.S.C. 2011 
                    et seq.
                    Dated: October 5, 2026.
For the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Michelle Hayes,
Chief, Advanced Reactor Licensing Branch 2, Division of Advanced Reactor Licensing, Office of Advanced Reactors.

articles.title: Wilkes-Barre Terminal Railway Company-Acquisition and Operation Exemption-Luzerne County Redevelopment Authority and Luzerne County Rail Corporation
articles.full_text:
Wilkes-Barre Terminal Railway Company (WBT), a noncarrier, has filed a verified notice of exemption under 49 CFR 1150.31 to acquire approximately 59.65 miles of rail line (the Line) from the Luzerne County Redevelopment Authority (LCRA) and the operating rights from LCRA's non-operating subsidiary Luzerne County Rail Corporation (LCRC), in Luzerne County, Pa. The Line consists of the following in-service segments: (1) the Dunmore Secondary Track, between milepost 6.5, at Avoca, Pa., and milepost 10+/− North side Montage Road Crossing, a distance of 4.5 miles; [] 
                    
                     (2) the Avoca Industrial Track, between milepost 1.8, at Number 7 Junction, and milepost 6.5, at Avoca, a distance of 4.7 miles,[] 
                    
                     including the connection with the track of Reading Blue Mountain & Northern Railroad Company (RBMN) between LB Junction and the switch of the Dunmore Secondary Track, a distance of 0.123 miles, and the Langcliff Connecting Track, between milepost 0.0, at Duryea, Pa., and the connection with Norfolk Southern Railway in the middle of York Avenue, at milepost 0.867, a distance of 0.867 miles; (3) the Suscon Industrial Track, between milepost 154.5, at Suscon, Pa., and milepost 158.7, at Hillside, Pa., a distance of 4.2 miles; (4) the Wilkes-Barre Secondary, between milepost 169.2, at Ashley, Pa., and milepost 185.5, at Pittston, Pa., a distance of 16.3 miles; (5) the GWBP Industrial Track, between milepost 0.0, at Ashley, and milepost 0.5, at Hanover Industrial Track, a distance of 0.5 miles; (6) the Brownsville Industrial Track, between milepost 0.0, at Hillside, and milepost 1.0, at Brownsville, Pa., a distance of 1.0 miles; (7) the Wilkes-Barre Industrial Track, between milepost 59.9, at Ferry Street, and milepost 62.9, at Wilkes-Barre, Pa., a distance of 3.0 miles; (8) the Kingston Industrial Track, between milepost 142.7, at Pittston Junction, and Railroad Station 8594+58, a distance of 8.1 miles; and (9) the D&H Wilkes-Barre Connector, from milepost A-208.08, Hudson Yard, to Conyngham Avenue, City of Wilkes-Barre, Pa., a distance of 2.5 miles; and (10) the APC line, between milepost 0.0 and 0.6 in Wilkes-Barre, a distance of 0.6 miles.
                
                    The Line consists of the following out-of-service segments: (1) the West Pittston Running Track, between milepost 0.0, at West Pittston, Pa., and milepost 3.0, at Harding, Pa., a distance of 3.0 miles, and between milepost 186.4, at West Pittston, and milepost 190.2, at Wyoming, Pa., a distance of 3.8 miles, and between milepost 194.2, at Wyoming, and milepost 194.4, in Kingston, Pa., a distance of 0.2 miles; (2) the Nanticoke Industrial Track, between milepost 0.0, at Ashley, and milepost 2.6 at Central Scrap, a distance of 2.6 miles; (3) the Harry E. Breaker Spur, between milepost 0.1, at Maltby Junction, and milepost 0.5, a distance of 0.4 miles; (4) the Miner's Mills Industrial Track, between milepost 173.6, at North Wilkes-Barre, and milepost 176.1, at Hudson, Pa., a distance of 2.5 miles; and (5) the Pettibone Branch, between milepost 0.0 and milepost 0.759, at Dorranceton, Pa., a distance of 0.759 miles.[] 
                    
                
According to the verified notice, WBT will enter into an agreement with LCRA and LCRC for the acquisition of the Line and operating rights to ensure continued rail service to customers. According to the verified notice, WBT will grant local trackage rights to RBMN to provide immediate rail service to customers on the Line following the expiration of the incumbent operator's lease.
                    This transaction is related to a concurrently filed verified notice of exemption in 
                    Reading Blue Mountain & Northern Railroad—Trackage Rights Exemption—Wilkes-Barre Terminal Railway,
                     Docket No. FD 36959, in which RBMN seeks authority to acquire local trackage rights over the in-service segments of the Line.[] 
                    
                
According to WBT, the proposed transaction does not contain an interchange commitment. WBT certifies that its projected annual revenues resulting from the transaction will not exceed $5 million and will not result in WBT's becoming a Class I or Class II rail carrier.
The earliest this transaction may be consummated is October 29, 2026, the effective date of the exemption (30 days after the verified notice was filed).
If the verified notice contains false or misleading information, the exemption is void ab initio. Petitions to revoke the exemption under 49 U.S.C. 10502(d) may be filed at any time. The filing of a petition to revoke will not automatically stay the effectiveness of the exemption. Petitions for stay must be filed no later than October 22, 2026 (at least seven days before the exemption becomes effective).
All pleadings, referring to Docket No. FD 36958, must be filed with the Surface Transportation Board either via e-filing on the Board's website or in writing addressed to 395 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20423-0001. In addition, a copy of each pleading must be served on WBT's representative, Justin J. Marks, Clark Hill PLC, 601 13th Street NW, Suite 600, Washington, DC 20005.
According to WBT, this action is categorically excluded from environmental review under 49 CFR 1105.6(c) and from historic preservation reporting requirements under 49 CFR 1105.8(b).
                    Board decisions and notices are available at 
                    www.stb.gov.
                    Decided: October 9, 2026.
By the Board, Anika S. Cooper, Chief Counsel, Office of Chief Counsel
Kenyatta Clay,
Clearance Clerk.

AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Direct final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate various statutory amendments. The rule reflects statutory changes making virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility, making clear that annual and sick leave provided under an authority outside of title 5, United States Code, may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, and excluding certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees from title 5 FMLA coverage.
DATES:
This rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026. If significant adverse comments are received, OPM will withdraw the affected provisions of this rule and issue a notice of proposed rulemaking.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments for this direct final rule within the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov/.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
All comments must be received by the end of the comment period for them to be considered. All comments and other submissions received generally will be posted on the internet at
regulations.gov
as they are received, without change, including any personal information provided. However, OPM retains discretion to redact personal or sensitive information, including but not limited to personal or sensitive information pertaining to third parties.
A summary of this rule may be found in the docket for this rulemaking at
www.regulations.gov.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Julie Ohr, Office of Personnel Management, Workforce Policy and Innovation, (202) 606-2858,
leavepolicy@opm.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This direct final rule amends OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in subpart L of part 630 of title 5, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) to reflect statutory changes enacted in January 2021 [1]
and December 2023.[2]
I. Background and Effect on Paid Parental Leave
The Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993, as amended, provides eligible employees with unpaid, job-protected leave for specified family and medical reasons under one of two separate and independent authorities, known as title I and title II of the FMLA. Title II of the FMLA added a Family and Medical Leave subchapter V in chapter 63 of title 5 of the United States Code (5 U.S.C. chapter 63, subchapter V), so it is generally referred to as “title 5 FMLA.” Title 5 FMLA is administered by OPM and applies to most Federal employees who are covered by the Federal leave system under 5 U.S.C. chapter 63 and some additional categories of employees. Title I of FMLA (non-title 5 FMLA), administered by the Department of Labor (DOL), applies to private sector employees, State and local Government employees, as well as some Federal employees (including employees of the U.S. Postal Service and the Postal Regulatory Commission). DOL's FMLA regulations are found in 29 CFR part 825 and should not be applied to employees covered by title 5 FMLA.
The 2021 and 2023 statutory amendments to the title 5 FMLA law also affect an employee's eligibility for paid parental leave (PPL). This is because PPL is a type of paid leave that is substituted for unpaid FMLA leave. Therefore, to be eligible for PPL, an employee must meet all eligibility requirements for use of FMLA leave as a covered “employee” (as defined in 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(A)) who has completed at least 12 months of qualifying service (as required by 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(B)). On August 10, 2020, OPM issued interim final FMLA/PPL regulations (85 FR 48075) to implement the Federal Employee Paid Leave Act (FEPLA),[3]
which authorizes the substitution of up to 12 weeks of PPL for unpaid FMLA leave granted in connection with the birth of an employee's son or daughter or the placement of a son or daughter with an employee for adoption or foster care. (See 5 U.S.C. 6382(a)(1)(A) and (B).) To implement FEPLA, OPM added new regulatory subpart Q (Paid Parental Leave) in 5 CFR part 630 and made necessary clarifications, changes, and additions in subpart L (Family and Medical Leave). Because the 2021 and 2023 statutory amendments addressed in this rule affect FMLA eligibility, those amendments (and this rule) therefore also affect PPL eligibility.

This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Bureau of the Fiscal Service, Department of the Treasury.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Department of the Treasury (“Treasury” or “we”) is issuing in final form amendments to the Uniform Offering Circular for the Sale and Issue of Marketable Book-Entry Treasury Bills, Notes, and Bonds (the “UOC” or “auction rules”). These amendments make technical changes to several sections of the UOC to remove outdated references and to be consistent with Treasury's current auction terminology. These amendments also modify the requirements for submitting noncompetitive customer bids, to require submitters to provide all
( printed page 65457)
customer bid information prior to the noncompetitive auction close.
DATES:
Effective date:
October 15, 2026.
Applicability Date:
The changes to 31 CFR 356.14 and 356.23 apply to all auctions of Treasury marketable securities beginning with the first Treasury marketable securities auction conducted using Treasury's upgraded auction system, which will be communicated to market participants in advance of the first applicable auction. All other changes apply as of the effective date.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Lori Santamorena, Kevin Hawkins, John Garrison, or Luisa Jou-Penchev, Office of Securities Regulatory Operations, Office of Financing, at
govsecreg@fiscal.treasury.gov
or 202-504-3632.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The UOC, codified at 31 CFR part 356, sets out the terms and conditions for the sale and issuance by Treasury to the public of marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.[1]
The UOC and the offering announcement for each auction represent a comprehensive statement of the auction terms and conditions.[2]
Discussion
In September 2026, Treasury announced plans to upgrade the auction system for the sale of marketable Treasury securities.[3]
In connection with the planned upgrade, Treasury is adopting amendments to the UOC to align auction rules with the planned system upgrades and to make other technical amendments for clarity and consistency.
First, Treasury is modifying the definitions of adjusted value, dated date, index ratio, issue date, and settlement amount in § 356.2 and making conforming changes to the examples in appendix B to part 356 with respect to references to dated date, issue date, and original issue date. The changes include a clarification that the denominator in the formula for calculating the index ratio is always the reference Consumer Price Index applicable for the original dated date. None of the changes affect the calculation of the adjusted value, index ratio, or settlement amount for inflation-protected securities.
Second, Treasury is making several changes to remove outdated references, by modifying (1) the definition of CUSIP number in § 356.2 to remove a reference to the name of the entity that formerly issued CUSIPs; (2) § 356.11(a)(2) to remove a reference to bids in paper form, which are no longer accepted; and (3) the header to Section III of appendix B to part 356 to remove a reference to inflation-indexed securities, which are now uniformly referred to as inflation-protected securities.
Third, Treasury is modifying the definitions of index, index rate, and noncompetitive bid in § 356.2, and modifying §§ 356.15, 356.20, and 356.21 to align references to the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin more closely to Treasury's current auction terminology. We are also modifying §§ 356.20 and 356.23 to use the words award and recognize in lieu of accept and tender. Section 356.23(b) is also revised to clarify that the list of information that may be included in the auction results is illustrative. These changes improve consistency between the auction rules, announcements, and results. Treasury will make corresponding adjustments to the terminology on future auction announcements and results press releases, as appropriate.
Fourth, Treasury is modifying the requirements for submitting noncompetitive customer bids in §§ 356.14(c) and (e) to require submitters to provide, prior to the noncompetitive auction close, each individual customer's name and bid amount for all noncompetitive bids. Submitters will no longer be able to submit a summary bid amount; the individual customer names and respective bid amounts may still be submitted in one consolidated list, but it must be received prior to the noncompetitive auction close. These changes, which will be effective with the planned system upgrades, will ensure all noncompetitive bid information is received prior to the noncompetitive auction close and will enable Treasury auction staff to finalize post-auction operations earlier in the day.
Finally, Treasury is removing references in §§ 356.23(a) and 356.31(a) to
http://www.treasurydirect.gov
and instead stating that we will make the auction results available on our website. This change will provide Treasury more administrative flexibility while maintaining public transparency regarding auction results.
Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
The APA generally imposes requirements on agency rulemakings related to notice, public comment, and delayed effective dates, under 5 U.S.C. 553. However, 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2) exempts matters relating to contracts from those requirements. The auction regulations relate to Treasury securities, which are contracts between Treasury and the owner of the security; therefore, the notice, public comment, and delayed effective date requirements of the APA do not apply to this final rule.
Regulatory Flexibility Act.
The provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, 5 U.S.C. 601et seq.,
do not apply to this final rule because, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2), this rule is not required to be issued with notice and opportunity for public comment.
Paperwork Reduction Act.
This final rule does not involve a collection of information. Therefore, the Paperwork Reduction Act, 44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.,
does not apply.
Congressional Review Act (CRA).
This final rule is not a major rule pursuant to the CRA, 5 U.S.C. 801et seq.
For the reasons set forth in the preamble, 31 CFR part 356 is amended as follows:
PART 356—SALE AND ISSUE OF MARKETABLE BOOK-ENTRY TREASURY BILLS, NOTES, AND BONDS (DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY CIRCULAR, FISCAL SERVICE SERIES NO. 1-93)
1. The authority citation for part 356 continues to read as follows:
2. Section 356.2 is amended by revising paragraph (2) of the definition of “Adjusted value” and the definitions of “CUSIP number,” “Dated date,” “Index,” “Index rate,” “Index ratio,” “Issue date,” “Noncompetitive bid,” and “Settlement amount” to read as follows:

AGENCY:
Office of Government Ethics.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendment.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is issuing this final rule to update the name of an existing departmental component that was previously designated for purposes of the one-year post-employment conflict of interest restriction for senior employees.
DATES:
Effective October 15, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kimberly L. Sikora Panza, Associate Counsel; Telephone: 202-482-9300; Email:
usoge@oge.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Substantive Discussion; Revision of Existing Departmental Component
The Director of OGE (Director) is authorized by 18 U.S.C. 207(h) to designate distinct and separate departmental or agency components in the executive branch for purposes of 18 U.S.C. 207(c), the one-year post-employment conflict of interest restriction for senior employees. Under 18 U.S.C. 207(h)(2), component designations do not apply to persons employed at a rate of pay specified in or fixed according to subchapter II of 5 U.S.C. chapter 53 (the Executive Schedule). Component designations are listed in appendix B to 5 CFR part 2641.
The representational bar of 18 U.S.C. 207(c) usually extends to the whole of any department or agency in which a former senior employee served in any capacity during the year prior to termination from a senior employee position. However, 18 U.S.C. 207(h) provides that whenever the Director “determines that an agency or bureau within a department or agency in the executive branch exercises functions which are distinct and separate from the remaining functions of the department or agency and that there exists no potential for use of undue influence or unfair advantage based on past Government service,” the Director shall by rule designate that agency or bureau as a separate component of that department or agency. As a result, a former senior employee who served in a designated component of a parent department or agency is barred from communicating to or making an appearance before any employee of that component, but is not barred as to any employee of the parent, of another designated component, or of any other agency or bureau of the parent that has not been designated. Likewise, a former senior employee who served in a “parent” department or agency is not barred by 18 U.S.C. 207(c) from making communications to or appearances before any employees of any designated component of that parent, but is barred as to employees of that parent or of other components that have not been separately designated.
The Director regularly reviews the component designations listed in appendix B to part 2641, and in consultation with the department or agency concerned, makes adjustments as are necessary. Pursuant to the procedures prescribed in 5 CFR 2641.302(e), the Department of Transportation has requested that OGE revise the name of one component currently listed in appendix B to part 2641. Specifically, the Department of Transportation requested that OGE revise Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation to read “Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation.” The revision is requested because the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation was legally renamed the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation as part of the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act (Section 512 of Division AA of P.L. 116-260), signed into law on December 27, 2020. The Department of Transportation advised that there have been no substantive changes to this component, and that the component name update is purely a technical change. OGE is therefore amending the Department of Transportation listing in appendix B to reflect the current name of this component.
The designation of Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation in appendix B to part 2641 was effective as of January 1, 1991.
See56 FR 3961. The component name change being made in this rule, which does not affect the underlying component designation date, is effective on October 15, 2026, the date this rule is published in the
Federal Register
.
II. Matters of Regulatory Procedure
Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553, as the Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I find that good cause exists for waiving the general requirements for notice of proposed rulemaking, opportunity for public comment, and a 30-day delayed effective date. As the change effectuated by the final rule is a minor, technical amendment to the current regulation, notice and comment is unnecessary. Furthermore, it is important and in the public interest that the component name change, which reflects the current organization of the concerned
( printed page 65450)
department be published in the
Federal Register
and take effect as promptly as possible.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
As Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I certify under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. chapter 6) that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it affects only Federal departments and agencies and current and former Federal employees.
Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. chapter 35) does not apply to this rule because it does not contain information collection requirements that require the approval of the Office of Management and Budget.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
For purposes of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. chapter 25, subchapter II), this rule will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments and will not result in increased expenditures by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (as adjusted for inflation) in any one year.
Congressional Review Act
The rule is not a major rule as defined in 5 U.S.C. chapter 8, Congressional Review of Agency Rulemaking.
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563
In promulgating this rule, the Office of Government Ethics has adhered to the regulatory philosophy and the applicable principles of regulation set forth in Executive Order 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review (58 FR 51735, Oct. 4, 1993) and Executive Order 13563, Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review (76 FR 3821, Jan. 21, 2011). Executive Orders 13563 and 12866 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select the regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity). Executive Order 13563 emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting flexibility.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
                    ACTION:
Final rule; correction.
                    SUMMARY:
                        EPA is making a correction to a final rule that appeared in the 
                        Federal Register
                         on August 26, 2026. The final rule established significant new use rules (SNURs) under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) for chemical substances that were the subject of premanufacture notices (PMNs) and Orders issued by EPA pursuant to TSCA. Subsequent to the publication, the Agency identified an error in a chemical name.
                    
                    DATES:
The final rule correction is effective on October 26, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        The docket for this action, identified under docket identification (ID) number EPA-HQ-OPPT-2024-0281-0081, is available online at 
                        https://www.regulations.gov
                         or in person at the Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics Docket (OPPT Docket) in the Environmental Protection Agency Docket Center (EPA/DC). Please review the visitor instructions and additional information about the docket available at 
                        https://www.epa.gov/dockets.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    This action corrects a regulatory amendment that was published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, (91 FR 54992 (FRL-12742-02-OCSPP)). The error to be corrected is listed here:
                
1. In the table of contents and heading and regulatory provision for 40 CFR 721.12151 the chemical name should be updated to edge oxidized carbon matrix (generic).
                    The Agency is not providing a public comment opportunity prior to promulgation of this technical correction, because such public comment is unnecessary under 
                    5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
                     of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The correction established in this action is non-substantive and would not alter the regulations established in the final rule. Therefore, pursuant to the APA section 553(b)(B), EPA finds good cause to promulgate this technical correction without notice and comment.
                
Corrections
                    In FR Doc. 2026-17400 appearing on pages 54996 and 54997 in the 
                    Federal Register
                     on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, the following corrections are made:
                
                    1. On page 54996, in the first column of the table of contents, the listing for § 721.12151 is corrected to read as follows: 
a. “Edge oxidized carbon matrix (generic).” 
                
                    2. On page 54997, in the third column, the section heading is corrected to read as follows: 
b. § 721.12151 Edge oxidized carbon matrix (generic) 
                
                    Dated: October 9, 2026.
Mary Elissa Reaves,
Director, Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics.
